text: Fortis Conference: Curacao, tax tradition Speech by Dr. E.D. Tromp, President, Bank of the Netherlands Antilles, on the occasion of the opening of: "Fortis Conference: Curacao, fiscal tradition " Curacao, Netherlands Antilles, November 8, 2007 Ladies and gentlemen, Boni bini, welcome to Curacao. It is a pleasure for me to address you today about the opportunities that our country offers in the field of international services. I hope that, at the end of my speech, I have been able to convince you that the Netherlands Antilles is a jurisdiction where you can do good business. I would like to thank Fortis Intertrust (Curacao) B.V., which I will hereinafter refer to as "Fortis" for the sake of convenience, for the invitation to give the opening speech today. In my speech, I will not go into depth about the tax aspects that our country offers, because other speakers will already discuss them in detail. Nevertheless, I will occasionally dwell on the possibilities in this area. Ladies and gentlemen, international financial services are one of the most important pillars of the Netherlands Antillean economy. As a financial centre, our country has been confronted with major challenges during the last 10 years. To paint a picture of this, I would therefore like to go back with you to the end of the nineties, where important developments have taken place. Not only for the Netherlands Antilles, but for financial centers worldwide. Towards the end of the nineties, financial centres had to deal with a multitude of complex and extensive initiatives by organisations such as the OECD, the Financial Action Task Force, the Financial Stability Forum and the European Union. Most of these initiatives concerned aspects relating to combating unfair competition in the field of taxation and money laundering. These are all aspects that expose us as a financial center to various risks, in particular reputational risks. At the same time as these developments, and partly as a result of a general awareness of the importance of financial services, competition between countries also increased with the aim of obtaining a larger share of this market. In addition, the establishment of an international financial centre, compared to other sectors, can be done relatively quickly without substantial physical investment, which also makes the introduction of this sector attractive for less developed countries. Competition exists not only between different countries but also within the industry itself. New developments in information technology and telecommunications have led to increasing competition between productive and service sectors, including the financial services sector. This sector has therefore experienced strong growth in recent decades due to, among other things, an increase in world trade, deregulation of local financial markets and globalisation in segments of the service sector. It is against this background that countries with a long-standing tradition of international financial services, including the Netherlands Antilles, had to rethink their strategies in order to maintain and strengthen their status as an international financial centre. The history of international financial services in the Netherlands Antilles goes back to the end of the thirties of the last century, when several large Dutch companies, anticipating a any war, transfer their assets to the Netherlands Antilles. After the end of the Second World War, the Netherlands Antillean Government created an attractive tax regime to preserve these companies. However, it was never the intention to make the Netherlands Antilles a completely tax-free paradise, because the country also wanted to enjoy some tax income. The government's efforts paid off. By the mid-60s, the Netherlands Antilles, and in particular Curacao, had developed into a renowned international financial center. Despite competition from surrounding countries and islands that used a tax-free regime, Curacao still managed to distinguish itself. Factors such as political and social stability, free movement of capital, presence of highly qualified personnel, a convenient location with good connections and communication opportunities and the presence of related services such as banking, legal, tax and accounting services played a role. As another important advantage, the connection with the Dutch part of the Kingdom was also experienced. However, this boom in our financial sector came to an abrupt halt with the termination of the tax treaty with the United States and the abolition of the US Foreign Witholding Tax in 1985. This meant the end of all kinds of highly profitable international financial activities in Curacao. Other factors contributing to this downward trend were the gradual terminations of other tax treaties with the Netherlands Antilles and the increasing competition from other tax-free jurisdictions. Ladies and gentlemen, despite the continuing decline in activities, our financial services sector managed to maintain an important position in the economy of the Netherlands Antilles. The total contribution of this sector to the economy of the Netherlands Antilles currently amounts to almost 8% of the Gross Domestic Product. The tax revenues of this sector amount to about 4% of GDP and more than 5% of the labour force is employed in this sector. During the period 2000-2006, this sector generated on average almost 14% of the foreign exchange income of the Netherlands Antilles. The international financial sector in the Netherlands Antilles consists of banks, insurance companies and other financial and service institutions that together manage, roughly estimated, a total of 36 billion dollars in assets, of which more than 96% is attributable to the banking sector. The international financial sector also contributes indirectly to the Netherlands Antillean economy through positive spillover effects on other sectors such as trade, tourism, telecommunications and transport. Other sectors also benefit from the publicity associated with promoting our financial services, ultimately resulting in additional foreign investment in our economy. It is also worth mentioning the role that the sector can play in the development of the capital market, in particular the establishment of a stock exchange. Finally, the relatively high incomes in this sector translate into higher local spending, which benefits the construction sector and trade, among others. In addition to the direct and indirect contribution of international financial services to our economy, the sector is also broadening the economic base of the Netherlands Antilles. Like other economies in the Caribbean, the Netherlands Antillean economy characterizes itself as a small and open economy, which makes it vulnerable to external factors. For example, we are also heavily dependent on tourism and are constantly exploring other possibilities to diversify our economy. Greater diversification of our economy can lead to a reduction in risks, which in turn will lead to new financial developments. Caribbean countries would do well to try to diversify their economies through knowledge-based service industries that specialize in high-value-added activities. The higher productivity associated with this will have a more permanent effect on the longer-term growth prospects. Ladies and gentlemen, you will agree with me that we must maintain and continue to strengthen our financial sector, given the relatively large contribution to our economy. Crucial to this are continuous efforts to strengthen our international competitive position, with the ultimate goal of becoming and remaining more attractive as an international financial center. Here there is a task for all of us and not just the Government. There are several conditions that, in my opinion, are essential for obtaining the status of an attractive international financial centre and for successfully maintaining that status once acquired. I will briefly review the most important conditions with you.  One of the most important conditions is macroeconomic and political stability. Sound and sustainable macroeconomic policies support the stability of the financial system. No less important is political stability. It promotes investor confidence in all sectors of the economy, but in particular in the international financial sector, due to its global nature.  Another important condition is a strong tax and legal infrastructure. A strong legal system is characterized by respect for property and other rights, compliance with agreements, an efficient, reliable, independent and credible legal system with a quick settlement of procedures. It is essential that the tax and legal infrastructure of the financial sector adapts adequately to the continuous developments in the international financial world. This implies the development and timely adaptation of relevant legislation.  No less important for a solid financial sector is the availability of qualified personnel. Access to a pool of skilled workers with legal, tax, controlling, administrative and management expertise is therefore crucial.  Furthermore, good communication opportunities and support services are also important factors for a successful international financial centre. The importance of this is underlined by the need for quickly available and effective information from parties operating in the market.  As a last, but certainly no less important condition, the presence of an adequate supervisory regime can be mentioned, which ensures a healthy financial system with strong banks, institutional investors and other financial service providers. The supervisory regime should, on the one hand, support economic development and growth and, on the other hand, safeguard financial stability and the interests of investors and depositors. However, supervision must be such that it can also respond quickly and effectively to changes in the financial world. The Bank of the Netherlands Antilles is responsible for the supervision of the financial sector in the Netherlands Antilles. Under the supervision of the Bank are commercial banks, savings funds, insurance companies, company pension funds, investment companies, credit unions, trust offices, administrators and insurance intermediaries. In total, it concerns about 500 institutions. As an international financial centre, we are highly dependent on an adequately functioning financial system. The Bank is therefore continuously engaged in increasing financial stability and minimising systemic risks by performing the supervisory task assigned to it by law as optimally as possible. Continuous efforts in a search for the best possible methods to strengthen the Netherlands Antillean financial sector are therefore no stranger to the Bank. The most important thing is to increase the quality of supervision in which high integrity standards, sound professional competence, sound management and healthy business operations are central. In my opinion, there is no alternative to proper supervision. Good supervision promotes a high quality of service, it ensures the preservation of the reputation of the sector and the maintenance of financial stability. I am also aware that over-regulation may impair the ability of our jurisdiction to maintain a competitive position as an international financial centre. It is therefore imperative that a balance is struck between the adequacy and effectiveness of rules and legislation on the one hand and the underlying risks to which our financial sector is exposed on the other. Ladies and gentlemen, at the beginning of my speech I said that the Netherlands Antilles has a lot to offer you. You will agree with me that, nevertheless, we cannot and must not sit still. The competition is closely following developments with us and will price us out of the market in no time if we do not remain alert. In my opinion, Fortis' initiative to hold this seminar in Curacao comes at the right time. In the international financial services sector, innovation plays an important role. If you want to stay ahead of the competition, you have to invest in the development of new products and also promote these products in the right way. During this seminar Fortis will introduce you to a number of new products. I welcome the way in which this introduction takes place. This way is typical of a company like Fortis, which has managed to position itself as one of the largest players in the financial sector worldwide. I therefore congratulate Fortis on the success it has already achieved and express the hope that this success will be continued in the future. I am convinced that there is a role for all of us in creating an honest and reliable financial sector in which honest people and companies operate creatively and energetically. The economic and social value of such an environment is unlimited in the long run. It remains for me to wish you a fruitful seminar and a pleasant stay on our island. Thank you for your attention.
text_original: Fortis Conference: Curacao, fiscale traditie http://www.centralbank.cw/uploads/images/Emsley%20Tromp.jpg Toespraak Dr. E.D. Tromp, President, Bank van de Nederlandse Antillen, ter gelegenheid van de opening van: <d2>Fortis Conference: Cura<8d>ao, fiscale traditie <d3> Cura<8d>ao, Nederlandse Antillen, 8 november, 2007 Dames en heren, Boni bini, welkom op Cura<8d>ao. Het is voor mij een genoegen u vandaag toe te mogen spreken over de mogelijkheden die ons land biedt op het gebied van internationale dienstverlening. Ik hoop dat ik, aan het eind van mijn betoog, u ervan heb kunnen overtuigen dat de Nederlandse Antillen een jurisdictie is waar u goed zaken kunt doen. Ik dank Fortis Intertrust (Cura<8d>ao) B.V, die ik hierna voor het gemak <d2>Fortis<d3> zal noemen, hartelijk voor de uitnodiging om vandaag de openingsrede te mogen uitspreken. Ik zal in mijn betoog niet diep ingaan op de fiscale aspecten die ons land biedt, omdat andere sprekers daar al uitgebreid op zullen ingaan. Niettemin zal ik af en toe even stilstaan bij de mogelijkheden op dit gebied. Dames en heren, de internationale financi<91>le dienstverlening is <8e><8e>n van de belangrijkste pijlers van de Nederlands-Antilliaanse economie. Ons land werd als financieel centrum gedurende de laatste 10 jaar met grote uitdagingen geconfronteerd. Om een beeld hiervan te schetsen wil ik daarom even met u teruggaan naar het eind van de jaren negentig, waar zich belangrijke ontwikkelingen hebben voorgedaan. Niet alleen voor de Nederlandse Antillen, maar voor financi<91>le centra wereldwijd. Tegen het einde van de jaren negentig kregen financi<91>le centra te maken met een hoeveelheid van complexe en omvangrijke initiatieven van organisaties zoals de OECD, de Financial Action Task Force, het Financial Stability Forum en de Europese Unie. Het merendeel van deze initiatieven betrof aspecten op het gebied van het bestrijden van oneerlijke concurrentie op belastinggebied en het witwassen van gelden. Dit zijn allemaal aspecten die ons als financieel centrum blootstellen aan verschillende risico<d5>s, in het bijzonder reputatie risico<d5>s. Tegelijk met deze ontwikkelingen, en mede als gevolg van een algemene bewustwording van het belang van de financi<91>le dienstverlening, nam ook de concurrentie tussen landen toe met als doel het verkrijgen van een groter deel van deze markt. Daar komt bij dat het oprichten van een internationaal financieel centrum, vergeleken met andere sectoren, relatief snel kan gebeuren zonder substanti<91>le fysieke investeringen, hetgeen de introductie van deze sector ook aantrekkelijk maakt voor minder ontwikkelde landen. Concurrentie bestaat niet alleen tussen verschillende landen maar ook binnen de industrie zelf. Nieuwe ontwikkelingen op het gebied van informatie technologie en telecommunicatie hebben geleid tot een toenemende concurrentie tussen productieve en dienstverlenende sectoren, inclusief de financi<91>le dienstverlenende sector. Deze sector onderging de laatste decennia dan ook een sterke groei door onder andere een toename in de wereldhandel, deregulering van locale financi<91>le markten en globalisering in segmenten van de dienstverlenende sector. Het is dan ook tegen deze achtergrond dat landen met een jarenlange traditie van internationale financi<91>le dienstverlening, de Nederlandse Antillen hieronder begrepen, hun strategie<91>n moesten heroverwegen teneinde hun status als internationaal financieel centrum te handhaven en te versterken. De geschiedenis van de internationale financi<91>le dienstverlening in de Nederlandse Antillen gaat terug tot het einde van de jaren dertig van de vorige eeuw, toen verschillende grote Nederlandse ondernemingen, anticiperend op een eventuele oorlog, hun activa naar de Nederlandse Antillen overhevelden. Na afloop van de Tweede Wereldoorlog cre<91>erde de Nederlands-Antilliaanse Overheid een aantrekkelijk fiscaal regime om deze ondernemingen te behouden. Het was echter nimmer de bedoeling om van de Nederlandse Antillen een geheel belastingvrij paradijs te maken, want het land wenste immers ook enig belastinginkomen te genieten. De inspanningen van de Overheid loonden zich. Halverwege de jaren 60 hadden de Nederlandse Antillen, en in het bijzonder Cura<8d>ao, zich ontwikkeld tot een gerenommeerd internationaal financieel centrum. Ondanks concurrentie van omringende landen en eilanden die een belastingvrij regime hanteerden, wist Cura<8d>ao zich toch te onderscheiden. Hierbij speelden factoren een rol als politieke en sociale stabiliteit, vrij verkeer van kapitaal, aanwezigheid van hoog gekwalificeerd personeel, een gunstige locatie met goede verbindingen en communicatiemogelijkheden en de aanwezigheid van gerelateerde diensten zoals bancaire, juridische, fiscale en accountantsdiensten. Als ander belangrijk voordeel werd ook de band met het Nederlandse deel van het Koninkrijk ervaren. Echter, deze bloei in onze financi<91>le sector kwam abrupt tot stilstand bij de be<91>indiging van het belastingverdrag met de Verenigde Staten en de afschaffing van de <d4>US Foreign Witholding Tax<d5> in 1985. Dit betekende het einde van allerlei zeer winstgevende internationale financi<91>le activiteiten op Cura<8d>ao. Andere factoren die bijdroegen aan deze neerwaartse trend waren de geleidelijke be<91>indigingen van andere belastingverdragen met de Nederlandse Antillen en de toenemende concurrentie van andere belastingvrije jurisdicties. Dames en heren, ondanks de voortgaande afname van de activiteiten wist onze financi<91>le dienstverlenende sector toch een belangrijke positie te behouden in de economie van de Nederlandse Antillen. De totale bijdrage van deze sector aan de economie van de Nederlandse Antillen bedraagt momenteel bijna 8% van het Bruto Binnenlands Product. De belastinginkomsten van deze sector bedragen ongeveer 4% van het BBP en meer dan 5% van de beroepsbevolking is in deze sector werkzaam. Gedurende de periode 2000-2006 genereerde deze sector gemiddeld bijna 14% van de deviezeninkomsten van de Nederlandse Antillen. De internationale financi<91>le sector in de Nederlandse Antillen bestaat uit banken, verzekeringsmaatschappijen en andere financi<91>le en dienstverlenende instellingen die samen, ruw geschat, een totaal van 36 miljard dollar aan vermogen beheren, waarvan ruim 96% toe te schrijven is aan de bancaire sector. De internationale financi<91>le sector draagt ook indirect bij aan de Nederlands-Antilliaanse economie via positieve overloopeffecten op andere sectoren zoals de handel, de toeristische sector, telecommunicatie en transport. Van de publiciteit die gepaard gaat met het promoten van onze financi<91>le dienstverlening profiteren ook andere sectoren, hetgeen uiteindelijk resulteert in additionele buitenlandse investeringen in onze economie. Noemenswaardig is verder de rol die de sector kan spelen in de ontwikkeling van de kapitaalmarkt, in het bijzonder de opzet van een effectenbeurs. Ten slotte vertalen de relatief hoge inkomens in deze sector zich in hogere lokale bestedingen, waarvan ondermeer de bouwsector en de handel profiteren. Naast de door mij genoemde directe en indirecte bijdrage van de internationale financi<91>le dienstverlening aan onze economie, verbreedt de sector ook de economische basis van de Nederlandse Antillen. Gelijk andere economie<91>n in het Caribische gebied, karakteriseert de Nederlands-Antilliaanse economie zich als een kleine en open economie, hetgeen haar kwetsbaar maakt voor externe factoren. Ook wij zijn bijvoorbeeld sterk afhankelijk van het toerisme en zijn continu bezig andere mogelijkheden te onderzoeken om onze economie te diversifiseren. Een grotere diversificatie van onze economie kan tot verlaging van risico<d5>s leiden, hetgeen weer nieuwe financi<91>le ontwikkelingen mee zal brengen. Caribische landen doen er dan ook goed aan om te proberen hun economie<91>n te diversifici<91>ren middels op kennis gebaseerde dienstverlenende industrie<91>n die zich specialiseren in activiteiten met een hoge toegevoegde waarde. De hogere productiviteit die hiermee gepaard gaat zal een meer permanent effect hebben op de groeivooruitzichten op langere termijn. Dames en heren, u zult het met mij eens zijn dat wij onze financi<91>le sector moeten behouden en moeten blijven versterken, gelet reeds op de relatief grote bijdrage aan onze economie. Cruciaal hiervoor zijn voortdurende inspanningen om onze internationale concurrentiepositie te versterken, met als uiteindelijk doel aantrekkelijker te worden <8e>n te blijven als een internationaal financieel centrum. Hier is een taak weggelegd voor ons allen en niet alleen de Overheid. Er zijn verschillende voorwaarden die naar mijn mening essentieel zijn voor het verkrijgen van de status van aantrekkelijk internationaal financieel centrum en om die eenmaal verworven status succesvol te behouden. Ik zal de belangrijkste voorwaarden kort met u nalopen. 1. Tot <8e><8e>n van de belangrijkste voorwaarden behoren de macro economische en politieke stabiliteit. Een gezond en duurzaam macro economisch beleid ondersteunt de stabiliteit van het financi<91>le systeem. Niet minder belangrijk is de politieke stabiliteit. Die bevordert het vertrouwen van investeerders in alle sectoren van de economie, maar in het bijzonder in de internationale financi<91>le sector, dit vanwege haar mondiale karakter. 2. Een andere belangrijke voorwaarde is een sterke fiscale en juridische infrastructuur. Een sterk juridisch systeem kenmerkt zich door respect voor eigendom en andere rechten, het naleven van overeenkomsten, een effici<91>nt, betrouwbaar, onafhankelijk en geloofwaardig rechtssysteem met een snelle afdoening van procedures. Het is hierbij essentieel dat de fiscale en juridische infrastructuur van de financi<91>le sector zich adequaat aanpast aan de voortdurende ontwikkelingen in de internationale financi<91>le wereld. Dit impliceert de ontwikkeling en tijdige aanpassing van relevante wetgeving. 3. Niet minder belangrijk voor een solide financi<91>le sector is de beschikbaarheid van gekwalificeerd personeel. Toegang tot een pool van bekwame arbeidskrachten met juridische, fiscale, controlerende, administratieve en management expertise is daarom cruciaal. 4. Voorts zijn ook goede communicatiemogelijkheden en ondersteunende dienstverlening belangrijke factoren voor een succesvol internationaal financieel centrum. Het belang hiervan wordt onderstreept door de behoefte aan snel beschikbare en effectieve informatie van in de markt opererende partijen. 5. Als laatste, maar zeker niet minder belangrijke voorwaarde, kan de aanwezigheid van een adequaat toezichtregime genoemd worden, dat toeziet op een gezond financieel systeem met sterke banken, institutionele beleggers en andere financi<91>le dienstverleners. Het toezichtregime dient aan de ene kant economische ontwikkeling en groei te ondersteunen en aan de andere kant financi<91>le stabiliteit en de belangen van investeerders en deposanten te waarborgen. Het toezicht dient echter zodanig te zijn dat het ook snel en doelmatig kan inspelen op de veranderingen in de financi<91>le wereld. De Bank van de Nederlandse Antillen is verantwoordelijk voor het toezicht op de financi<91>le sector in de Nederlandse Antillen. Onder het toezicht van de Bank staan commerci<91>le banken, spaarfondsen, verzekeringsmaatschappijen, ondernemingspensioenfondsen, beleggingsmaatschappijen, kredietverenigingen, trustkantoren, administrateurs en assurantiebemiddelaars. In totaal gaat het om ongeveer 500 instellingen. Als internationaal financieel centrum zijn wij sterk afhankelijk van een adequaat functionerend financieel systeem. De Bank is daarom continu bezig met het verhogen van de financi<91>le stabiliteit en het minimaliseren van systeemrisico<d5>s door de haar wettelijk opgedragen toezichttaak zo optimaal mogelijk uit te oefenen. Voortdurende inspanningen in een zoektocht naar de best mogelijke methoden om de Nederlands-Antilliaanse financi<91>le sector te versterken, zijn de Bank dan ook niet vreemd. Voorop staat het verhogen van de kwaliteit van het toezicht waarbij hoge integriteitnormen, gedegen vakbekwaamheid, degelijk bestuur en gezonde bedrijfsvoering centraal staan. Naar mijn mening bestaat er geen alternatief voor goed toezicht. Goed toezicht bevordert een hoge kwaliteit van dienstverlening, het waarborgt het behoud van de reputatie van de sector en het behoud van financi<91>le stabiliteit. Ik ben mij er ook van bewust dat overregulering afbreuk kan doen aan het vermogen van onze jurisdictie om een concurrerende positie als internationaal financieel centrum te handhaven. Het is daarom imperatief dat er een evenwicht wordt gevonden tussen de adequaatheid en effectiviteit van regels en wetgeving enerzijds en de onderliggende risico<d5>s waaraan onze financi<91>le sector is blootgesteld anderzijds. Dames en heren, aan het begin van mijn betoog stelde ik dat de Nederlandse Antillen u veel te bieden heeft. U zult het met mij eens zijn dat we desondanks niet stil kunnen en mogen zitten. De concurrentie volgt de ontwikkelingen bij ons op de voet en zal ons binnen de kortste keren uit de markt prijzen als we niet alert blijven. Het initiatief van Fortis om dit seminar op Cura<8d>ao te houden komt mijn inziens dan ook op het juiste moment. In de sector van de internationale financi<91>le dienstverlening speelt innovatie een belangrijke rol. Wil men de concurrent voor blijven, dan dient men te investeren in de ontwikkeling van nieuwe producten en deze producten ook op een juiste wijze promoten. Tijdens dit seminar zal Fortis u kennis laten maken met een aantal nieuwe producten. De wijze waarop deze kennismaking geschied juich ik toe. Deze wijze is typerend voor een bedrijf als Fortis, dat zich als <8e><8e>n van de grootste spelers in de financi<91>le sector, wereldwijd heeft weten te positioneren. Ik feliciteer Fortis dan ook met het reeds behaalde succes en spreek de wens uit dat dit succes in de toekomst zal worden gecontinueerd. Ik ben ervan overtuigd dat er een taak voor ons allen is weggelegd in het cre<91>ren van een integere en betrouwbare financi<91>le sector waarin integere personen en bedrijven creatief en voortvarend opereren. De economische en sociale waarde van een dergelijke omgeving is op de lange termijn onbegrensd. Rest mij nog u een vruchtbaar seminar en een prettig verblijf op ons eiland toe te wensen. Ik dank u voor uw aandacht.

Title: Christmas Speech on the occasion of the Christmas 2009 celebration of the Central Bank
CentralBank: Central Bank of Curaao and Sint Maarten
text: Developmental Challenges in a Small Economy: The Case of St. Maarten Speech by Dr. E. Tromp on the occasion of The State of the Economy Presentation, Philipsburg, St. Maarten March 20, 2008 Ladies and gentlemen, good evening, With pleasure I accepted the invitation from Commissioner Buncamper-Molanus to speak to you on the relevant theme d2Developmental Challenges in a Small Economyd3 at this event surrounding the presentation of the Economic Outlook 2008. St. Maarten is a very small economy, but a highly successful one as I shall demonstrate later. I shall begin my address this evening with an analysis of St. Maartend5s economy, which is growing at an impressive speed. In the second part of my address, I shall discuss with you some of the challenges of the constitutional changes that are ahead for the island. If managed well, these changes create enormous opportunities for high sustainable growth in the coming years. St. Maarten is the second largest economy of the Netherlands Antilles with a 20% share of total Gross Domestic Product, approximately 1.2 billion guilders. Although Curacaod5s 70% share is considerably bigger, St. Maartend5s economy has performed much better. Since the end of the economic recession in 2001, the economy of St. Maarten has grown by an annual average rate of 3.8% in real terms, compared to 1.8% for Bonaire, and a marginal 0.3% for Curacao. A preliminary estimate by the Central Bureau of Statistics indicates a real growth rate of 4.5% for St. Maarten for 2007. The islandd5s strong economic growth has been accompanied by a moderate rate of inflation, averaging 1.8%, but increasing to 2.3% in 2007. The higher- than- average inflation rate can be explained mainly by the impact of rising world oil prices. St. Maartend5s robust economic growth contributed to a decline in the unemployment rate, which reached 10.6% in 2007. This rate is better than the 12.0% in Curacao, but Bonaired5s unemployment rate was even lower at 7.8%. Youth unemployment still contrasted sharply with overall unemployment. With 26.0% of St. Maartend5s labor force in the age group of 15-24 unemployed, the island has the highest rate in the Netherlands Antilles; this figure compares to 24.2% in Curacao and 20.5% in Bonaire. Tourism is the dominant sector in St. Maartend5s economy and can be illustrated in various ways. In the National Accounts, tourism activities encompass the following sectors: Trade; Hotels & Restaurants; Transport, Storage & Communication; and Real Estate, Renting & Business Activities. Gross value added by these sectors comprises 56% of total business activities and 42% of Gross Domestic Product for the island. St. Maarten welcomes an impressive number of visitors each year. The number of stay-over visitors is approaching the 500,000 limit, and the number of cruise passengers has exceeded 1.4 million. In 2007, St. Maarten accounted for 56% of stay-over tourism and 76% of cruise tourism in the Netherlands Antilles. Tourism activities in St. Maarten generate approximately 1.2 billion guilders in foreign exchange revenues annually, representing 64% of total foreign exchange revenues from tourism in the Netherlands Antilles. However, these impressive figures are somewhat overshadowed by the disappointing visitor growth rates during the last two years. The number of stay-over visitors has remained about the same since 2005, while the number of cruise passengers declined in 2006 and remained almost unchanged in 2007. I think the main explanation for this development is that St. Maartend4s utilization of its tourism infrastructure has reached full capacity. Therefore, further growth can be attained only by expanding the tourism infrastructure. Investors seem to believe in the potential for further growth, as evidenced by the continued robust growth in construction activities indicated in a press release from the Central Bureau of Statistics and the Department of Economic Affairs of St. Maarten last month. Hotel room and time share capacity as well as cruise pier capacity are expanding, creating prospects for the resumption of growth in the number of visitors in the near future. Another explanation for the weak growth in tourism may be the weakening economy of the United States, from which more than half of St. Maartend5s tourists originate. In line with the weak tourism performance, the airport and the harbor of St. Maarten also showed weak growth in 2007. Nevertheless, the Princess Juliana International Airport remained the busiest of the Netherlands Antilles airports, with 1.7 million passengers handled, half of all passengers handled in the Netherlands Antilles. With the recent modernization and expansion of St. Maartend5s airport, its capacity has increased to 2.5 million passengers per year. Thus, this part of St. Maartend5s infrastructure is capable of absorbing the anticipated recovery in tourism growth without any problems. Harbor growth is expected to resume once the expansion of the cruise pier and the container and freight handling facilities have been completed. I support the vision behind the expansion of the container and freight handling facilities to develop the harbor as a transit point for the distribution of goods to the neighboring islands. This is a step towards the necessary diversification of the economy. Ladies and gentlemen, I am an optimist who worries a lot. Therefore, allow me now to draw your attention to some of the weaknesses of St. Maartend5s economy. The most obvious weakness is the heavy reliance on one principal economic activity, namely, tourism. This characteristic is typical of most small island economies. However, such heavy reliance on a single activity enhances the business cycle and makes the economy more susceptible to external shocks. Reducing reliance on one main economic activity requires diversification. A small island economy like St. Maarten has, of course, only limited possibilities for diversifying its economy given, among other things, its lack of natural resources, scarcity of land, and small domestic market. This situation should not, however, prevent its policymakers and the business sector from coming up with creative ideas. Enhancing the regional distribution function of St. Maarten is a viable policy to pursue. The current expansion of the harbor and the recent expansion of the airport fully support this policy. I also note the idea of developing an international financial and business services sector on the island, an activity worth further exploration. However, a word of caution is at order: the daunting list of challenges that surround the creation of a world class international financial and business services sector requires a world class regulatory infrastructure and the institutional capacity to implement it, which may prove to be overly ambitious given your resource constraints. Another major weakness in St. Maartend5s economy is that the public infrastructure has not kept up with the expansion of the economy, either physically or socially. The physical dimension can be illustrated by the insufficient capacity of the road infrastructure, which has resulted in structural congestion most of the day. Electricity and water production cannot keep up with demand, causing frequent power outages and water shortages. The increasing amount of solid and liquid waste generated by businesses and the public cannot be processed effectively, which has created a growing burden for the environment. Some examples of the social dimension are shortages of schools, daycare facilities, and social housing, an understaffed police force, and an inadequate penitentiary system. These shortcomings have resulted in a rising crime rate and increasing social imbalances, aggravated by the illegal immigration issue. Ladies and gentlemen, I mention these weaknesses since they are a good starting point for discussing with you the challenges of the constitutional changes for the future country of St. Maarten. One of the many tasks in preparing the island for its new constitutional status is addressing effectively the observed economic and social imbalances to create a sound social-economic basis for durable balanced growth in the years ahead. With the new status comes the responsibility to govern the new country with a population anxious to reap the benefits of the new status. It is not a question of survival, but a challenge of leadership. Like inheritance, success can be invested productively or not. The question therefore to be answered is whether you are investing in what it takes to continue to build on the existing foundation while using the new status to meet the challenges that will await you as a new country within the Kingdom. According to the current thinking, St. Maarten is scheduled to become a country on December 15 of this year. However, almost all stakeholders realize that this date is not attainable. I strongly believe that a thorough preparation with all the laws and institutions in place is crucial for a viable start as a country. Until this process is completed, assumption of the new constitutional status is bound to create more issues than it solves for Sint Maarten. The number of issues that must be addressed before St. Maarten can become a country are quite overwhelming, but they also create unique opportunities to correct the administrative, economic, and social ills on the island with broad technical and financial support from the Dutch government. Given the time constraint, I have selected a few to discuss with you in more detail. These are the design of an effective and efficient government apparatus, sound government finances, and the future of the monetary system and financial supervision. Let me start with the design of the government apparatus. The present dual layer of government has created numerous inefficiencies, promoted tensions between the central and island administrations, and frequently undermined the effective implementation of policies. Now that St. Maarten is becoming a country and the central government is being dismantled, a unique opportunity is created for the design of a new effective and efficient government apparatus. First, the government tasks must be defined, including the tasks that are taken over from the central government. Second, legislation on which to base the implementation of the government tasks must be prepared and approved. I think current legislation will generally be adequate, complemented with the necessary amendments. Third, the government apparatus must be adequately staffed in accordance with the requirements in the job description of each position. The positions can be filled from the current pool of civil servants of the island as well as from the central government, if necessary complemented with additional training. Positions that remain open should be advertised and filled with external candidates. Current civil servants who do not meet the job requirements and cannot be properly retrained should seek employment in the private sector after receiving adequate redundancy payments. Finally, the principles of good governance should be embedded in the new government apparatus to guarantee effective and responsible spending of the citizensd5 tax money, efficient high quality services to the public, and effective sanctions for misconduct and abuse. The second issue that must be addressed and about which I would like to share my views with you is sound public finances. Based on the relatively few occasions that St. Maarten has approached the central government for financial assistance, it appears that it has been able to bring expenditures in line with revenues. However, its budgetary process has been rather murky. The government has operated quite a few times without an approved budget for part of the year. Regular progress reports on the implementation of the budget have been absent. Budget audits have been delayed for years. Although the government is legally not allowed to borrow, St. Maarten has built up a considerable debt, sometimes created because of creative financing constructions. I do not want to suggest that St. Maarten has a monopoly on weak fiscal discipline and deviation from the budget legislation. The other islands and even the central government also have failed in this area. I only mention it as an illustration that a drastic change is necessary in how we approach the public finances in preparing for the islandd5s future status as a country. In the agreement between the central government, the governments of Curacao and St. Maarten, and the Dutch government of November 2, 2006, better known as the d2Slotverklaringd3, the parties explicitly underscored the importance of starting the new constitutional status with a financially sound position. To arrive at this position, the Dutch government is prepared to take over a substantial part of the debt of the entities. In the new situation, St. Maarten will be granted the long desired authority to borrow but within strict limits. The maximum allowed outstanding debt will be bound to an interest burden rule, prescribing that the interest expenses in the budget may not exceed 5% of the average revenues of the preceding three years. It is still not very clear what this means for St. Maarten. First, the interest burden must be calculated from an estimated revenue base of the country of St. Maarten. Second, the room for borrowing depends also on the loans that remain the responsibility of St. Maarten after the debt relief. But I think it is safe to conclude that there will be some opportunity to borrow. The debt relief and authority to borrow are bound by strict conditions and control that will substantially enhance fiscal discipline and transparency. First, the current account of the budget may not have a deficit and must be presented in a multi-annual framework. Second, interest expenses may not exceed the 5% rule. Third, the recommendations of the Financial Position working group on improvement of the financial management and control must be implemented as planned. Fourth, the entire budgetary process from preparation of the draft budget to the accountability of its implementation is subject to supervision by an autonomous supervisory authority that will monitor whether the budget rules and other agreements are met, suggest corrective actions in case of deviations, and report its findings on a regular basis. I can imagine that this new approach to the public finances will be a culture shock for the island. In the beginning, it will create frequent tensions with the supervisory authority; the recent experiences of Bonaire, Saba, and St. Eustatius serve as an example here. It is for this reason that I have always been a strong proponent of a complete debt relief with the simultaneous elimination of the authority to borrow. But be as it may, we have to go through this period of adaptation to arrive at lasting sound public finances, a conditio sine qua non for building up a viable country with a prosperous future for its citizens. The third issue Id5d like to bring forward, and one which I keep particularly close at heart as a central banker, is the future of our monetary system and financial sector supervision in the new constitutional arrangement. The d2Slotverklaringd3 explicitly states that there will be one central bank for Curacao and St. Maarten responsible for monetary, financial, and integrity supervision based on one set of laws. Rationally considered, I fully subscribe to this statement. It means that the current central bank will be broadly maintained, continuing its good reputation and credibility in safeguarding the stability of the monetary and financial system. I believe this is very important in light of the uncertainties surrounding the numerous changes that will take place on the road toward the new constitutional status of the islands. In addition, with a common central bank, economies of scale can be maintained with regard to the high costs of highly educated staff and modern information and communication infrastructure. Moreover, a common central bank will provide a larger common economic area with broader economic diversification, which may dampen the impact of a shock occurring on one of the islands. If Curacao and St. Maarten as autonomous countries share a common central bank and currency, they join a monetary union. Since autonomous countries have their own policy responsibilities, a monetary union requires a high degree of policy coordination and harmony to ensure a balanced and effective monetary policy. In addition, a well functioning monetary union requires free movement of goods, services, capital, and labor between the countries. These requirements may be difficult to reconcile with the desire for more autonomy by Curacao and St. Maarten since this desire was the main driving force behind opting for country status. Ladies and gentlemen, I do not like to sound like the rooster who claims credit for the sunrise. We must begin however, with the understanding that strong political commitment is required to give up some of the newly won policy autonomy in the interest of a stable and effective monetary union. If we fail to comprehend this, we will not be able to create a stable monetary environment conducive to growth and stability. We will need to work well together because we have a great challenge before us. It is our own incredible success that we face. As mentioned, like inheritance the new found opportunities can be exploited successfully or be squandered. Though not far from inconceivable, the inevitable question becomes; if the politicians cannot come to an agreement on a common central bank, what will be the next best alternative? Given the current financial architecture, Curacao will likely continue the current central bank, although its revenue base will shrink as a result of the division of the foreign exchange reserves with St. Maarten and the omission of income from the issuance of banknotes and currency transactions with banks in St. Maarten. With respect to St. Maarten, it is the question whether it will be able to sustain a full- fledged central bank in a profitable way. The smallness of the economy simply hampers the generation of enough income to cover the operational costs. This means that the central bank will become dependent on government financing, which will undermine its independence and, hence, credibility. In general, a central bank contributes to government revenues, not the other way around. Actually, St. Maarten does not need its own monetary policy. An own monetary policy and consequently an own central bank is needed only if you have your own currency. Because the US dollar is used so widely, official dollarization is an efficient and feasible alternative. Hence, dollarization eliminates the need for a central bank. In effect, you will elect to distribute the seignorage profit to the public at large rather than having it accrued to the central bank. The other question which we cannot deflect is: What about the supervision of the financial sector? Since most financial institutions in St. Maarten are subsidiaries or branches of foreign-based institutions, the central bank of the respective parent company continues to include them in its supervision. Instead of setting up its own supervisory authority, which will suffer from large diseconomies of scale, it would be much more efficient and effective for St. Maarten to outsource the supervision of the financial sector to the central bank of the parent institution. Ladies and gentlemen, St. Maartend5s economic development can be considered a success story. However, it is accompanied by increasing imbalances in the public domain, which will eventually undermine the sustainability of the current growth. The preparations for the new constitutional status provide a unique opportunity to address these imbalances effectively, helped by financial and technical support from the Dutch government. An efficient and effective government apparatus, sound public finances, a stable monetary system, good governance, and adequate financial sector supervision are essential elements for building a viable and prosperous country. The road towards this goal is marred with obstacles and setbacks. You have to be careful not to devote too much energy to achieve the new status while neglecting to strengthen the foundation and creating the institutional capacity to govern the new country. Our history is too simple and the facts, as they are commonly understood, not so clear. Governing a country is a matter of no little importance. It requires skills different than those for governing an island territory. Dismissing this may prove to be more disruptive than helpful. You will be leading a nation in a world riven with economic, financial and environmental challenges. What happens anywhere can matter everywhere. But, the people of St. Maarten have proven resilient when the going gets tough, and I am convinced that they are tough enough to get going. Thank you for your attention.

Title: Challenges in Social Housing
CentralBank: Central Bank of Curaao and Sint Maarten
text: Challenges in social housing Speech by Drs. A.G. Romero, director, on the occasion of the 10th anniversary of the Caneye Foundation. Sint Maarten, 22 May 2008 1.Inleiding Ladies and gentlemen, it is a great pleasure for me to address you today about, among other things, the financing of social housing, but from the perspective of relatively small island economies. First of all, let me warmly congratulate the directors of the "Caneye" Foundation on the celebration of their 10th anniversary, which is characterized by cooperation in the field of social housing and its financing. Last month I was invited to give a lecture here about the starting position of the island of St. Maarten within the new political structure of the Kingdom. Then the presentation was about a new tax system for the country of St. Maarten. Today we are going to talk about a completely different matter and possibly I was only asked as a non-expert in the field of social housing because I was allowed to serve as treasurer for 5 years on the board of the Fundashon Kas Popular (FKP) in Curacao. It is very striking that in the discussion about the new political relations in the 'West' so little attention is paid to the subject of (social) housing. Perhaps, with the lectures that will be reviewed today, we can offer the administrators possible solutions to this important policy issue. In recent years, local and Dutch administrators have paid a lot of attention to the issue of poverty on our islands. I have the impression that the discussion has mainly focused on the social minimum income that is desirable, and the spread of poverty across our neighbourhoods. However, poverty is a complex phenomenon that not only concerns the level of income but also matters such as housing and living environment. Often the poor part of our society lives in poor quality housing without basic services such as water and electricity. In many cases, one has to share love and suffering with each other with too many people in a relatively small living space. In this respect, poverty on our islands is not much different from that on the (egg) countries in the region or in South America. In my opinion, more attention should also be paid to this dimension of poverty at administrative level. Today I would like to discuss with you a number of factors that are symptomatic of the poverty problems on our islands. And then I mainly focus on social housing and the financing thereof. Some of the issues that are central to this are:  Is only the government responsible for financing social housing?  In addition to public funds, are there other alternative sources of financing for social housing?  Is there a role for financial institutions in this ? An important "issue" that currently has the international financial world in its grip is the problem of mortgages in the "subprime" market in the U.S. In short, this problem means that since mid-2007, financial institutions have been confronted with an increase in poorly running loans at the bottom of the mortgage market. These loans have been granted in the past to borrowers who, in respect of:  their credit history;  schuldendienst en inkomensverhouding en  mortgage debt versus the value of the real estate in principle, do not meet the qualification of well-to-do (reliable and secure) borrowers. On the subprime market, the loans were usually financed with variable interest rates. The U.S. real estate market has seen significant price declines since mid-2005, leaving many families too deeply in debt. This causes an ever-increasing problem for financial institutions of having to write off loans because there is insufficient coverage for the outstanding debts. After all, their assets have fallen considerably in value, which means that the coverage of outstanding loans with real estate can no longer be guaranteed with certainty in the future. Houses are now being auctioned en masse by financial institutions in the US. Financial institutions in Europe and elsewhere are also confronted with gigantic write-offs on their 'subprime' mortgages. Recently, in its publication "World Economic Outlook"[1] and the Financial Stability Forum [2], the IMF estimated that the problem of the subprime market now amounts to around 1,000 billion. It is precisely low-income families who have fallen victim to this due to a fall in interest rates on mortgages in the period 2002-2005 in combination with rising prices of real estate. The problem in the "subprime market" shows that the financing of housing for families from the low-income groups is a complex matter.  Social housing and housing in an international perspective.[ 3] Social housing almost always involves houses and buildings that are owned or already owned by the governments or government institutions and that are offered for rent or for sale to the socially weak or the low-income groups in society. So the role of the government (or governments), whether or not through separate legal entities created for this purpose, is always crucial. This is certainly not surprising given that guaranteeing a dignified existence of the socially weaker in society is seen as a responsibility of the government in most countries. The socially weaker must be protected from deep poverty or, to put it another way, they must therefore be able to count on the necessary basic services. Affordable accommodation is one of these basic facilities. An international comparison shows that countries fulfil the government's responsibility for social housing in different ways. I would like to discuss with you the social housing and the role of the government in this, in a number of countries. Namely the USA, France, Germany and Spain. If we now look at the history of social housing in the US, we see how social housing has been tackled there for decades. Around the 30s of the last century, people in the US started building high apartment towers with the intention of helping many people find housing at a brisk pace. It was mostly the poor families who were the first to qualify for this type of housing. These families were allocated a home at affordable or subsidized rents. However, concentrating many people from the lowest income groups in high-rise apartment buildings in certain neighborhoods without proper social counseling has resulted in a rise in crime in the U.S. and the formation of the so-called Ghetto neighborhoods that we all know from documentaries and films. Something that was initially well-intentioned turned out wrong in practice. The social unrest in Ghettos became untenable at some point. As a result, the policy in the field of social housing was revised in the 90s. In 1993, for example, the "Home and Urban Development (HOPE)" programme was launched. This aims to renovate social housing projects but, in contrast to the past, a clear vision of the future has been developed. One is take more account of the fact that the new tenants and existing residents must come from different income groups. It is expected that this will result in less crime and illegality in the neighborhoods in question. The government therefore tries to reduce or even avoid social problems by bringing people from different income groups together. From this period also stems the government's plan to have social housing financed and built by the private sector. Through so-called 'special housing programmes', the government offers income subsidies to potential tenants/residents in order to acquire affordable accommodation. In France, social housing received a huge boost after the 2nd world war when many families in the big cities were left without proper shelter due to the damage, as a result of the war violence. This created a scarcity of affordable housing. This, in turn, resulted in a huge increase in rents in almost all housing categories. The government in France was then forced to respond quickly. In a short time, the government stamped one social housing project after another off the ground. The building plans that got off the ground at the time included the rapid construction of so-called "Habitation a Loyer Modere" (HLM) with the aim of building affordable rental housing. It should be noted that the HLM homes were used by politicians to attract and bind voters behind the political parties. Despite the many political discussions and corruption scandals that characterized the HLM construction projects, this form of building is still very common and popular in France. In France, too, it has become clear - and this has recently become painfully apparent in certain neighbourhoods around Paris - that concentrating many groups of people from the socially weaker backgrounds in neighbourhoods and residential buildings can lead to riots, social excesses and confrontations. In Germany, the development of building social housing began between 1925 and 1930 in the cities of Berlin, Cologne and Frankfurt Am Main. The immediate reason for the construction of public housing was the inhumane living conditions of the poor in the period after the 1st World War in Germany. In 1919, the German Constitution (Weimar Constitution) even included that people had the right to clean and affordable housing. Most social housing projects were located in and around the big cities and were so-called low-rise homes that did not go beyond 5 high. These homes were equipped with all conveniences and basic amenities such as electricity and water. With the rise of the Nazis in 1933, these large social housing projects came to an end in Germany because the founders and architects involved in these projects had a different political vision than the rulers of the time. As a result, these experts were forced to leave their country. As a result, some of the expertise and knowledge in the field of social housing has also been withdrawn from Nazi Germany. Today, social housing in Germany has been completely privatized. The German government uses the subsidy instruments to guarantee social housing for the lowest income groups. Until the 80s of the last century, the German government provided subsidies to private construction companies for the construction of social housing. In addition, the government did set some conditions such as maximum rental rates that the companies were allowed to apply. Nowadays, the government no longer subsidizes the construction of social housing, but direct rent and income subsidies are provided to individual families from the low-income groups. The Spanish "Viviendas de Proteccion Publicas" are similar to the German social housing projects. The construction of this "Viviendas de Proteccion Publica" had its heyday during the dictatorship of General F.Franco (1936-1975). After the fall of the dictatorship, government investment in social housing declined dramatically. At the same time, the mentality of the Spaniards changed, in the sense that they considered renting social housing to be below their means. Moreover, this could be associated with the dictatorship of General Franco. As a result, the people themselves proceeded to build modest family homes. In recent years, due to the enormous increase in the prices of real estate in Spain, the pressure on the government has become increasingly to start building government-subsidized housing again. This 'tour d'horizon' around building for poor families and people with low incomes was deliberately done here to show some characteristics of social housing in certain parts of the world. Typically, the history of social housing in the world shows that the government has played and in some countries still plays an important role in the design, construction and financing of these homes. Without the financial contribution of the government or without subsidizing the rents in this sector, these homes for the poor families would not have got off the ground. We are now facing major challenges worldwide - the islands of the Netherlands Antilles, not excluding them, to find out what alternative forms of financing are possible to ensure a dignified home for families from the lower social classes in the coming years.  Social housing: St. Maarten and Curacao We will now briefly outline the conditions surrounding social housing on our islands with a view to identifying trends that we have also encountered in the US and Europe. Let's start with the situation on the island of St. Maarten. In 1996, after hurricanes "Luis" and "Marilyn", the "St.Maarten Housing Development Foundation" (SMHDF) was established[4]. It was at that time, thanks to the good cooperation with the Fundashon Kas Popular (FKP) in Curacao, that the SMHDF quickly got off the ground. The SMHDF is non-profit-making and, as an NGO, has the main objective of building and renovating social housing ("public housing") on St. Maarten. At present, the SMHDF is responsible for three social housing projects:  The Belvedere project where 474 are managed;  The "Emergency homes" consisting of 200 houses built across the island ;  The "Senior Homes" for the elderly consisting of 24 houses. The Belvedere project and the "Senior Homes" were established in the late 90s and were made possible by the support and funding of the Ministry of The Interior and Kingdom Affairs for a total amount from NAf. 57.7 Mio. ( 32 million). Here on St. Maarten, too, we see that, just like in other countries, the large social housing projects are built and financed with (Dutch) government funds. On Curacao, the "Fundashon Kas Popular" was founded in 1978[5] on the initiative of the Dutch government, the Antillean government and the island territory of Curacao. The foundation aims to improve public housing on Curacao. The first housing projects realized by the FKP were:  Public housing construction Tera Kora (phase 1) 157 Houses  Public house construction Soto 35 Houses  Public house construction Barber 39 Properties  Public house construction Westpunt 25 Houses The first "FKP" homes were completed in 1980. In total, approximately 110 housing projects on Curacao have been carried out by the FKP to date, which amounts to approximately 4400 homes. The FKP is currently working on the following housing projects:  Sapate Phase 2, 121 homes  Rifwaterstraat /Arubastraat 23 homes  Sapate phase III 40 homes For the period 2008 to 2010, the following projects are still planned by the FKP. Table 1 projects planned for the period 2008-2010 by FKP. Project location Number of properties Brakkeput 102 Sapate 50 Fortuna Pariba Zuid 50 Moontjeweg 180 Triangelweg 84 Total 466 In total, 466 homes will be delivered in 3 years. Despite the impressive track record and the stormy construction activities in Curacao in recent decades, the need for housing is still great. For example, approximately 6000 people are still registered as home seekers in the files of the FKP. This shows that the demand for social housing is still much higher than the supply. A better match between the supply and demand of social housing is therefore necessary.  Become forms of financing for Social Housing? In the introduction I just indicated that the financial world is currently in a state of shock due to the troubles surrounding mortgage products in the subprime market in the US. It is mainly people from the low-income groups who are involved in the problems surrounding the non-fulfilment of the repayment obligations on mortgage loans. As a result, it is the homes of these people that are being auctioned as a result of the crisis. The problems in the subprime market make finding alternative forms of financing urgent. At the same time, the negative publicity surrounding this mortgage crisis makes finding alternatives difficult. As a result of the mortgage crisis, we are seeing a global trend of tightening the conditions for granting mortgages by financial institutions  often imposed by international regulators. This puts the financing of borderline cases and especially of the low-income groups at risk. Despite this negative note, I do think that there is enough room to come up with private initiatives so that housing cooperatives on our islands - such as the "Caneye" Foundation - can continue to build and finance social housing projects. In the following I will mention some thoughts that may sound strange but that can certainly be used to do more.  Alternative forms of financing. A first perspective to secure financing of social housing relies to a large extent on public sector resources. This is the so-called target payments of the government (governments). This form of financing is not new and was/is applied as previously mentioned in Europe and the US. Unfortunately, direct financing of social housing by the government is often accompanied by political interference, unreasonable action and improper use and misappropriation of public funds. As a result, this form of financing often clashes with the rules of Good Governance ("Good Governance"). This is also the reason why, in my opinion, we should avoid this form of financing as much as possible. Moreover, the direct financing of social housing with public funds from the budget is something that no longer fits in with our time. In the case of St. Maarten and Curacao, it has also been agreed that in the future political structure, public finances will be put in order. The question then is whether sufficient resources are available to meet this purpose of social housing. Another form of financing that should be examined in the near future is the provision of housing subsidies to individual families. This form of financing can hardly be continued in the coming years in the coming years in the same way as it is currently the case with regard to the future countries st. Maarten and Curacao. This is for the simple reason that the new countries in the Kingdom have made agreements with the Netherlands about the maximum debts and related financing deficits. Limiting the debt build-up to a maximum by means of the interest burden standard therefore means that it is difficult to continue financing social housing in its current form. The provision of housing benefit by the government will certainly be subject to maximums. Contrary to what is often seen in other countries including countries in the region, we currently have an underdeveloped market for housing finance in the social sector on our islands. Especially in Latin and Central America, social housing is partly financed by the issuance of special bonds ("Bonos hipotecarios") by housing cooperatives. The advantage for the buyers of these special bonds is that they receive a special tax ruling so that the interest received on these bonds can be touched partly or entirely tax-free. As a result, the financiers increase their return after tax. At the same time, these "bonos hipotecarios" are used by the housing foundations to offer the socially weaker groups who are eligible for this financing for building their own home at a relatively low mortgage interest rate. This is certainly an alternative that needs to be further developed and investigated for mortgages to the socially weaker in our society. A fourth possibility to make the financing of social housing more attractive is a philosophy that the FKP has consistently applied in the past. In doing so, the housing corporation performs both commercial activities on which a market return can in fact be earned and social housing that is offered at a return that is lower than the market. The underlying idea is that there is a 'cross-subsidy' from commercial housing to social housing. At the moment, a return on the mortgage market of 7% is real on our islands. If sufficient projects can be financed at this rate on the commercial market segment, it is quite conceivable that social housing can eventually be financed at 5% interest. This alternative combined with the idea of a "bonos hipotecarios" issued by the housing corporations can certainly offer a solution for the financing of social housing.  Challenges in a competitive mortgage market One of the most important challenges facing housing corporations and associations on our islands in the coming years is the intensified competition in the mortgage market between traditional banks and institutional investors. In recent years, we have seen on all islands that mortgage interest rates are falling sharply. There are two reasons for this. Firstly, in the competition, banks have used interest rates as a tool to expand their customer base. Furthermore, due to the entry of new players in the mortgage market, the interest rate on mortgages has systematically fallen. About 10 years ago, people paid 9% to 10% on mortgage loans at the moment the interest rate has already dropped to 7% and even 6.5%. As a result, housing corporations that used to advertise "attractive" mortgage rates of 7 to 8% to the middle-income groups are no longer competitive with these rates due to the competition on the islands. They also have to offer a mortgage interest rate of 5 to 6% to be ahead of the competition. Secondly, liquidity in the global economy has risen so much that a fall in interest rates has become almost inevitable. In part, this means that insurers, pension funds and banks will start providing loans at very competitive interest rates if they still want to make a reasonable return on their invested capital. For the housing corporations, this means that they can expect that the interest rate for the projects they want to finance with debt capital will also fall in the future. So there is certainly an advantage for the housing corporations to be achieved here. A third important development that is already having a negative effect on construction costs is the rising prices of construction products. Due to the sharp rise in prices in all kinds of markets, but especially in construction, building all types of homes has become considerably more expensive. For the common man this is no longer affordable, especially because we still import a large part of our construction goods from Europe. Due to the more expensive euro, this has become almost unaffordable.  Development of new products by housing corporations. So far, we have only looked at how social housing can be financed at attractive rates in the future. What has remained underexposed is the question of how housing associations themselves can develop new products so that they can generate more revenue in the future. The philosophy must therefore be that the housing corporations must grow from within by developing and offering new products. In other words, "the mentality must be rolling up its sleeves to bring money into the coffers". That is why I also looked at what the housing corporations themselves can do to increase their revenues in the future. I will mention here some factors that can possibly increase yields. Providing services for the valuation of homes. In my opinion, this is a product that fits very closely with the current activities of the housing corporations. They pre-eminently have a group of technical experts who, with little additional training, can be hired by private individuals for objective valuations of homes. Providing services in advising and supervising construction projects. This product is also not a "far from my bed" activity for the housing associations. Nowadays, these actions on the commercial market, must be realized quite quickly. And who better to do that than the technicians who are professionally engaged in social housing at the housing corporation and building homes for sale in the commercial market. Building housing for the target group of returning graduates In my opinion, there is a wasteland here that needs to be mined and for which commercial rents can easily be charged. Young people who have studied abroad are used to living independently. When they return to the islands, they also want to live independently. They then encountered the problem of finding a home that is affordable. In almost all cases, the rents here are above the social minimum. In the Netherlands, the so-called growth mortgages have been developed for this target group. This is a product that can also be offered by the local housing corporations and with which additional commercial revenues can be obtained. He advise, build and supervise school maintenance projects. In Curacao, these activities are housed in a special foundation (Stichting Onderhoud Scholen or SOS). This gives a form of further fragmentation of activities that are all housed can be in one organization. It is possible that additional work and revenues can be generated for the housing corporations to this end, thereby reducing their dependence on the government . This is certainly not an exhaustive list of activities that can be developed by housing associations to generate additional revenues and that are worth investigating further. There are two more points regarding the BES islands that require attention in the coming years. In the new political relations within the Kingdom, the BES islands will be given a special status of "Public Entities". It has already been agreed that these islands will have a closer relationship with organizations in the Netherlands. This will undoubtedly be the case for the social housing problem. Now the cooperation between the various island housing corporations can be called good. A good example of this is this initiative of "Caneye". In the near future, I expect that this cooperation will only become closer. Isn't it possible here to look together with the Dutch housing corporations at possibilities of closer cooperation in, for example, the Dutch Social Housing Guarantee Fund? In any case, this could mean that cheaper funds for social housing on the BES islands become available. In addition, low mortgage rates are not excluded in the future. This certainly benefits not only the BES islands but also the FKP on Curacao and SMHDF on St. Maarten. Smhdf and FKP can benefit from this collaboration, for example, by at least making expertise and "know-how" available . Secondly, cooperation between social housing corporations and commercial financial institutions will be able to give an important boost to the development and financing of housing in general. Furthermore, the housing corporations must think very deeply about closer cooperation with financial institutions on the islands. In one way or another, opportunities must be sought to reduce the funding costs of social housing. Only then and only then can housing corporations quickly and cheaply revive the problem of building for the socially weak in society.  Conclusions and recommendations To conclude this long presentation, I would like to say the following. We have talked about the history of social housing and its financing. Looking back at social housing showed that, first and foremost, government involvement has been important all over the world. This involvement took shape in the first phase through target payments from public funds for the design and construction of homes with basic services such as electricity and water. In the second phase, the government gave subsidies to families from the lowest income groups in order to obtain affordable housing. In addition, housing corporations were encouraged to build themselves with financial support from the government for the socially weak within existing commercial projects. It has become clear from our "tour d' horizon" that social housing has been accompanied by corruption, political favoritism and the improper use of public funds. Moreover, bringing together people from a particular social environment has only exacerbated crime and illegal trafficking in neighbourhoods where predominantly social housing was concentrated. Instead of fighting poverty, it seemed that the government itself contributed to organizing crime and corruption. So it was high time to take a different approach to this matter. At the end of the 90s, almost everywhere, one sees that the authorities have started to change their strategy with regard to social housing. This resulted in the construction of large housing projects in which families from different income groups and professions were brought together with the aim of combating crime. In the knowledge that the governments in our country will have to put their finances in order in the coming years, the housing corporations will have to change their strategy. I have described two alternatives for reducing dependence on government on social housing. One alternative has to do with the treatise of "Bonos Hipotecarios" which is widely used in our region to make the financing of design and construction cheaper. The aim of this instrument is to reduce the cost of financing social housing. Ergo this allows the interest rate for the financing of social housing to go down and it becomes possible to offer financing below the market interest rate. This can be done by means of special issuance of instruments that have an advantageous 'ruling' for taxes . A second alternative to make social housing affordable and financeable is to "cross-subsidize" housing in the commercial sector at market rates to housing for the socially less fortunate in society. These commercial proceeds could be used by the housing corporations to finance social housing and rent. This is a strategy that the FKP in Curacao has been using for years with varying degrees of success. So it needs to be further refined to make it a permanent success factor. Finally, I have put forward a number of alternatives so that the housing corporations can enter the market with new products to generate income. One scenario is that the housing corporations themselves enter the market to make valuations of projects and homes for the government but also for commercial projects. At the time of a construction 'tree' as we now experience on almost all islands, this will certainly not be a breeze. A second form of 'out of the box thinking' is the design and supervision of housing for the market sector. This brings in a certain additional stream of income that can be used by housing corporations to finance social housing at reasonable rates. In addition, housing corporations can expand their range of activities with the construction of housing for young recent graduates and the maintenance of schools. I express the hope that the "Caneye" Foundation will become an even closer whole in the coming years so that the island organizations can continue to benefit from the added value of working together and building a better future in the "West".
