K<98>rsou i Sint Maarten lo bira paisnan out<97>nomo den Reino, mi<8e>ntras Bonaire, Saba i Sint Eustatius lo ha<96>a un laso mas direkto ku Hulanda. Un di e komponentenan di mas importante den e proseso di desmantelashon di Antianan Hulandes ta e saneamentu di debe ku a kumins<87> na yan<9f>ari di 2009 pa gobi<8f>rnu sentral i pa gobi<8f>rnu insular di K<98>rsou, na aprel di 2009. E proseso aki a kumins<87> despues ku e dos entidatnan menshon<87> a kumpli ku e eksigenshanan stipul<87>. E eksigensianan aki tabata enser<87>, entre otro, presupuesto balans<87>, i fortifikashon di e maneho finansiero. A estables<8e> e Hunta di Supervishon Finansiero, <98>f College Financieel Toezicht (CFT), pa supervis<87> finansa di e diferente gobi<8f>rnunan temporalmente. Konforme e programa di saneamentu di debe, gobi<8f>rnu hulandes lo paga 70% di gastunan di interes i 100% di debenan ku ta vense, te ora aproksimadamente 70% di e debenan ku mester a paga ainda na final di 2005 ta kansel<87>. Den kuadro di e saneamentu di debe, Hulanda a transfer<92> aproksimadamente 835 mion florin pa durante di 2009. Manera ya mi a menshon<87> ta entre otro danki na e saneamentu di debe aki ku Antianan Hulandes kontrali na mayoria pais den region, a konos<8e> un kresementu ekon<97>miko. Komo resultado di e saneamentu di debe ak<92>, e tasa di debe kompar<87> ku Produkto Interno Bruto lo baha konsiderablemente durante 2009. For di 1994 diferente intento i esfuerso a w<98>rdu has<92> pa balans<87> e presupuesto di gobi<8f>rnu i konsekuentemente redus<92> nos debe p<9c>bliko. Nos a implement<87> entre otro rekomendashonnan di Fondo Monetario Internashonal, Komishon Debe Nashonal i Banko di Desaroyo Internashonal. Gobi<8f>rnu a hasi intento pa entre otro redus<92> gastunan di p<8f>rsonal i supsidionan. Ademas a subi ingresonan di gobi<8f>rnu dor di introdus<92> <d2>omzetbelasting<d3> i mehor<87> i optimalis<87> kobransa di impuesto. L<87>stimamente den hopi kaso e rekomendashonnan no a w<98>rdu aplik<87> integralmente. Konsekuentemente e medidanan aki no tabata sufisiente pa realis<87> un presupuesto balans<87> i redus<92> nos debe p<9c>bliko. Sin saneamentu di debe, K<98>rsou lo a drenta e status di pais out<97>nomo den Reino ku un debe igual na 94% di nos produkto interno bruto. Esaki lo a nifik<87> un debe di mas o m<8e>nos 30 mil florin pa kada habitante di K<98>rsou, - for di esun di mas h<97>ben te esun di edat mas avans<87>. Den e kaso di Sint Maarten, e isla aki lo a bira pais out<97>nomo den Reino ku un debe igual na 80% di e produkto interno bruto. Esaki lo tabata un debe di mas o m<8e>nos 18 mil florin pa kada habitante di e isla aki. Indudablemente, e debe aki lo a result<87> den un posishon di salida debil pa tantu K<98>rsou komo Sint Maarten. Konsekuentemente e futuro paisnan lo no tabatin espasio riba na presupuesto pa mehor<87> nan situashon sosio-ekon<97>miko. Saneamentu di debe al kontrario ta duna nos e oportunidat pa fortifik<87> nos ekonomia. Pa e motibu ey, e aktual diskushon tokante kontinuashon di e proseso di saneamentu di debe ta hopi preokupante. Ta importante pa den e diskushon aki nos para ketu na e implikashon di deskontinuashon di e proseso aki. Deskontinuashon di e proseso aki lo nifik<87> ku K<98>rsou i Sint Maarten lo mester a tuma medidanan dr<87>stiko pa di e forma ey realis<87> un presupuesto balans<87>, redus<92> e debe p<9d>bliko i logra un desaroyo sosio-ekon<97>miko duradero. Un alternativa pa saneamentu di debe ta oumento di impuesto. Den e kaso aki lo mester a oument<87> impuesto ku 90%. Indudablemente esaki ta un alternativa irealistiko ya ku e ta da<96>a nos klima di invershon i konsekuentemente stroba nos kresementu ekon<97>miko. Pues, kontinuashon di e proseso di saneamentu di debe ta krusial pa nos logra un desaroyo sosio-ekon<97>miko duradero. Apesar ku saneamentu di debe ta fortifik<87> nos ekonomia, e no ta solushon<87> tur nos problemanan. Den mayoria kaso e problemanan no ta pa falta di Hulanda of otro pais, sino ta origin<87> serka nos mes. Desaroyo sosio-ekon<97>miko duradero di nos pais ta reker<92> desishonnan krusial di nos banda. Por eh<8f>mpel e konstrukshon di un megapir na Caracasbaai, modernisashon di nos refineria, desaroyo di e <87>rea di Rif i Santa Barbara ta nos propio responsabilidat. Esaki no ta solamente responsabilidat di gobernantenan sino di nos tur. Erornan ku a w<98>rdu komet<8e> den pasado, jamas lo mester wordu ripit<92>. Apresiabel koleganan i invitadonan, un biaha mas mi ke felisit<87> un i tur presente pa nan aporte dun<87> na nos komunidat en general i na Banko Sentral en partikular durante di e a<96>a ku ta terminando. Laga nos sigui hasi nos m<87>ksimo esfuerso pa huntu nos sigui aport<87> na desaroyo duradero di nos islanan. Na n<98>mber di gerensia di Banko mi ke dese<87> boso tur un Felis Pasku i un A<96>a Nobo yen di dicha i prosperidat pa boso i boso famia.

Title: Farewell to the Dutch Minister of Finance, Mr Gerrit Zalm Introduction presented on the occasion of the farewell of the Dutch Minister of Finance, Gerrit Zalm
CentralBank: Central Bank of Curaao and Sint Maarten
text: The Challenges of the Financial Crisis and the Constitutional Changes for the Supervision of the Financial Sector Speech by Dr. Emsley Tromp, given during the seminar Future of Supervision in the Dutch Caribbean on 29 March 2010 Ladies and gentlemen, good afternoon, First of all, I would like to express my appreciation for the organization of this seminar by the Dutch Ministry of Finance. I think it is the first time that the supervisors of the financial sector of the Kingdom have met to discuss the future of supervision. The most important reason is of course the constitutional changes in our Kingdom and the consequences thereof for the organization of supervision in the various countries. In addition, we cannot ignore the global changes in the supervision of financial institutions following the biggest financial crisis since the Great Depression in the thirties of the last century. These global changes also determine to a large extent the future of supervision within the Kingdom. I would like to share my views with you on these two topics. I would like to start with the international financial crisis and the role of supervision in it. The causes of the financial crisis are many and, through a complex confluence of circumstances, we came close to a collapse of the international financial system. Strong intervention by central banks and governments worldwide has prevented this, but of course it should never have come to that. As a result of globalisation, ever larger, globally operating financial institutions have emerged, which have also become increasingly intertwined. As a result, systemic risk in the financial sector has increased sharply and a mortgage crisis in the United States could shake the global financial system. Within the Kingdom, the financial sector in the Netherlands has been hit considerably harder by the crisis than that in the Netherlands Antilles and Aruba. The Dutch state has had to come to the aid of various financial institutions to save them from ruin, which has even led to the nationalization of one of the largest banks. In the Netherlands Antilles and Aruba, financial institutions have of course also felt the effects of the crisis, such as the decline in the value of investment portfolios and the sharp fall in interest rates. However, due to the lower international orientation, the greater risk aversion and the supervisory policy of the BNA, our local financial institutions have not run into problems. The institutions active in international financial and business services have been hit harder by the financial crisis as a result of their strong international orientation. Partly due to the BNA's supervisory policy, no institutions have run into problems in this sector either, but activities have decreased. This has led to downsizing at various institutions, including staff redundancies. Ladies and gentlemen, we must realise that the supervision of the financial sector is always lagging behind. Developments in financial markets are moving at breakneck speed as a result of globalisation and advancing information technology. New, often very complex financial products are put on the market within a short period of time with the promise of attractive returns without the risks being sufficiently understood. As long as the returns are realized, criticism remains. However, this situation changes rapidly when things go wrong and investors have to significantly depreciate their investments, as has happened with the derivatives based on US mortgages. Inadequate risk management, a skewed remuneration policy and insufficient expertise or alertness of supervisory directors of financial institutions are some of the factors that contributed to the crisis. These factors were also identified by the supervisors and brought to the attention of the responsible ministers. However, adequate intervention was hampered by legal restrictions. Legislative processes are generally slow. This certainly applies to supervisory legislation, which is often very technical and hardly appeals to the ordinary citizen. So it is not a subject that can be used to score politically. A crisis often turns out to be a unique opportunity to get legislation passed quickly. In the case of the Netherlands Antilles, I can illustrate this with an example. In the early nineties, we had been working on a legislative proposal to significantly modernise the existing supervisory legislation in order to be able to take more adequate action at credit institutions. At a certain point, a large Venezuelan bank got into trouble that was also active as an offshore bank in the Netherlands Antilles. This crisis contributed to the bill being debated and adopted within a short period of time. The then introduced national banking and credit supervision ordinance 1994 gave the BNA the necessary legal instruments to intervene more effectively in supervised institutions. This enabled problems at institutions to be identified more quickly and adequately addressed to prevent worse. Hopefully, the recent financial crisis will also ensure the prompt treatment and adoption of the shortly presented harmonisation legislation on supervision. This further modernises the statutory supervisory instruments in accordance with international standards and guidelines and harmonises corresponding provisions in the various supervisory laws. This is of great importance in order to maintain and expand our position as an international financial services centre. There are a number of lessons to be learned from the financial crisis, which could lead to changes in the supervision of the financial sector internationally and within the Kingdom in the short term in order to significantly reduce the chance of recurrence. A selection of the most important proposals circulating. First, the role of risk management in financial institutions needs to be substantially strengthened. In the period before the crisis, risk management was increasingly marginalised in favour of the big profit-promising new complex financial products. The BIS, the IMF and the Maas Committee, among others, have already made proposals to strengthen risk management by, among other things, setting up a risk committee at financial institutions and by giving the supervisory board and the internal auditor a greater role in assessing risks. Secondly, the remuneration policy of the top financial institutions is in urgent need of revision. Worldwide, remuneration practices have come under intense criticism and initiatives have been taken to regulate them. In particular, the variable component linked to the profitability of the institution has led to excesses due to the wrong incentives and should be limited. The necessary adjustments will be translated into general guidelines for remuneration policy in the financial sector. Thirdly, a more balanced balance of interests within the policies of financial institutions is necessary. Before the crisis, the interests of shareholders were paramount and the interests of other stakeholders, such as savers and employees, were often subordinate to this. The management of the institution is primarily responsible for a balanced balance of interests, in which long-term value creation must be paramount. In this area, too, valuable recommendations have been made by international organisations and committees on the basis of which concrete guidelines can be issued. Fourthly, the capital buffers of financial institutions need to be strengthened. Colleague Wellink in the BIS context, the IMF and the Financial Stability Board, among others, are working proposals. Higher capital requirements in general are envisaged, supplemented by additional requirements for large international institutions, which entail a so-called systemic risk. It also calls for mechanisms that make it compulsory to strengthen capital buffers in good times in order to absorb blows in bad times. Financial institutions need to become more resilient in times of crisis, so that governments no longer have to step in en masse to prevent the financial stability of a country from being undermined. Finally, I would like to mention the strengthening of corporate governance. In this context, strengthening supervision by the Supervisory Board plays a prominent role. In order to achieve this, the supervisory authority should test the expertise and independence of supervisory directors to a greater extent, audit and risk committees at financial institutions should be made mandatory and the functioning of the supervisory directors should be evaluated on a regular basis. Ladies and gentlemen, in order to maintain healthy international competitive relations and a level playing field, it is essential that supervisors worldwide cooperate closely with each other in the elaboration of the best practice proposals to be included in national laws and regulations for the supervision of financial institutions. International institutions, such as the BIS and the IMF, have a pioneering and coordinating role in this. Cooperation initiatives are also being developed regionally. In this context, the initiative to establish a European supervisory model along the lines outlined by the De Larosiere report can be mentioned. What appeals to me about this initiative is that the national supervisors remain responsible for the implementation of supervision. In addition to the national supervisors, there will be a European body that draws up binding policy rules, may act in a binding manner in the event of conflicts between national supervisors in the case of cross-border financial institutions and ensures a uniform application of laws and regulations. Descending to the Kingdom level, I advocate a similar supervisory structure, which I will explain in more detail for you. In addition to the challenges that the financial crisis has brought to the supervision of financial institutions worldwide, the political changes within the Kingdom also play a role closer to home. The current Netherlands Antilles of five islands ceases to exist. Curacao and St. Maarten become autonomous countries within the Kingdom, while Bonaire, Saba and St. Eustatius become part of the Netherlands. This new structure means that the importance of cross-border supervision, even if it takes place on a small scale within the Kingdom, is increasing. This requires a different organisation of supervision in order to continue to ensure its effectiveness and efficiency. In the current structure of the Kingdom, cross-border supervision also plays a role. This is the case , for example, between the Netherlands Antilles and Aruba, because several financial institutions with headquarters in Curacao also have branches in Aruba. There is also cross-border supervision between the Netherlands Antilles and the Netherlands; this mainly concerns institutions active in the international financial services sector. In order to better structure this common supervision, the Bank has already concluded several bilateral cooperation agreements with the Central Bank of Aruba and De Nederlandsche Bank in the past. The Central Bank of Aruba is concerned with the MOUs for the supervision of banking and credit institutions of 14 October 1998 and the supervision of the insurance sector of 3 April 2003. Prior to these MOUs, a protocol for periodic consultations between the two institutions was signed on 22 April 1998. An MOU for banking supervision was signed with De Nederlandsche Bank on 28 August 1997 and an MOU for the supervision of pension funds and insurance companies on 3 April 2002. In March 2008, cooperation between the Central Banks of the Kingdom was further expanded and intensified with the signing of a trilateral MOU. Specific areas of cooperation include integrity supervision, financial stability, supervision of the payment system, implementation of the amended Basel II capital agreement, statistics, strategic planning and budgeting, training and exchange of personnel. The cooperation focuses on support from De Nederlandsche Bank through the exchange of its extensive knowledge and experience in these areas with its Caribbean partners. Furthermore, the organization of the cooperation has been further formalized and consists of a Board of Governors, supported by a Technical Committee that is responsible for the implementation of agreements made and is assisted by a secretary. With this sketch of the evolution in cooperation between the central banks of the Kingdom, I want to illustrate that the step towards the organization of the supervision of financial institutions at Kingdom level is actually not a big one at all and follows logically from the increasingly close mutual cooperation. The set-up that I have in mind for this Kingdom supervisory body, which could, for example, be called the College of Kingdom Supervisors, therefore shows an analogy with the organization of the current trilateral cooperation. The Kingdom supervisory body will consist of the governors of the central banks in the Kingdom, who elect a chairman from among their number. This body will be assisted by a Technical Committee consisting of 3 members. Each central bank shall nominate one member, with the director in charge of supervision . The Technical Committee, supported by a secretariat, is responsible for the preparation and monitoring of timely implementation of laws and regulations in the field of financial supervision in line with international best practices, a level playing field with fair competition relations, and compliance with laws and regulations within the Kingdom. The elaboration of the necessary laws and regulations falls under the responsibility of an executive body, in which the deputy directors of the various supervisory disciplines sit. This body is also responsible for the actual implementation of the agreed policy and checks whether the laws and regulations in the countries of the Kingdom are complied with. The organisational structure of the supervision of financial institutions in the Kingdom that I have outlined will be able to guarantee compliance with international standards and the application of uniform rules within the Kingdom. For example, the current problems surrounding the negative FATF evaluation of the supervision of Aruba may no longer occur in the new supervisory structure. Furthermore, the proposed structure will promote the transparency and credibility of supervision. Moreover, it is to the kingdom's credit if all partners meet the international requirements with regard to financial supervision. In the context of the political changes in the Caribbean part of the Kingdom, intensive cooperation is already taking place between the supervisory authorities in the Netherlands Antilles and the Netherlands to ensure that the transition to the new situation runs as smoothly as possible. Although the political boundaries within the Kingdom will change, the financial sectors on the islands in the Caribbean part remain closely intertwined. Uniform laws, regulations and policies in the field of supervision of the financial institutions operating on the islands can then ensure that the supervisory burden for the institutions remains manageable and a "level playing field" can be maintained. Institutionalisation of the organisation of supervision in a Kingdom body can promote its sustainability. An example in this context is behavioural supervision, which has been commonplace in the Netherlands for some time but is still in its infancy in the Caribbean. Since the BES islands will fall under the responsibility of the Netherlands, the financial institutions on these islands will also have to deal with behavioural supervision. Thanks to the close cooperation within the Kingdom body, Curacao, St. Maarten and Aruba can then work in parallel with the BES islands, so that a "level playing field" can be maintained. Ladies and gentlemen, it is not so difficult to present an outline of how best to organise the supervision of the financial sector in the Kingdom. The real challenge lies in its concrete implementation, in which the necessary barriers must be overcome. For example, the laws and regulations in the field of supervision must be uniform as much as possible, but also take into account the diversity of the Kingdom partners. In other words, "unity in diversity." This principle is intended to ensure that supervision in all parts of the Kingdom complies with international standards, but leaves room for differences based on, for example, the structure and degree of development of the financial sector. In addition, in the new constitutional structure we will have to deal with four countries, four parliaments and four supervisory bodies. It will then not be an easy task to introduce almost uniform legislation at the same time in all parts of the Kingdom, which could jeopardise the intended "level playing field". I see an important preparatory and coordinating role for the Kingdom supervisory body here. Ladies and gentlemen, I look forward to a fruitful discussion with you about the future of supervision in the Dutch Caribbean in particular and the Kingdom in general. A future that is largely in our own hands. By working together even more intensively, we can face the challenges of the financial crisis and the constitutional changes for the supervision of financial institutions in the Kingdom with confidence. It is up to us to work out these challenges in a solid supervisory framework that contributes to sound financial institutions and financial stability in the countries of the Kingdom. Thank you for your attention and wish you a successful seminar.
text_original: De Uitdagingen van de Financiele Crisis en de Staatkundige Veranderingen voor het Toezicht op de Financiele Sector Toespraak van Dr. Emsley Tromp, gehouden tijdens het seminar Toekomst van het Toezicht in de Nederlandse Caribean op 29 maart 2010 Dames en heren, goedemiddag, Allereerst wil ik mijn waardering uitspreken voor het organiseren van dit seminar door het Nederlandse Ministerie van Financi<91>n. Het is volgens mij de eerste keer dat de toezichthouders op de financi<91>le sector van het Koninkrijk bijeenkomen om te discussi<91>ren over de toekomst van het toezicht. De belangrijkste aanleiding is uiteraard de constitutionele veranderingen in ons Koninkrijk en de gevolgen daarvan voor de inrichting van het toezicht in de onderscheiden landen. Daarnaast kunnen we niet voorbijgaan aan de mondiale veranderingen in het toezicht op financi<91>le instellingen naar aanleiding van de grootste financi<91>le crisis sinds de Grote Depressie in de jaren dertig van de vorige eeuw. Deze mondiale veranderingen bepalen ook in belangrijke mate de toekomst van het toezicht binnen het Koninkrijk. Over deze twee onderwerpen wil ik graag mijn visie met u delen. Ik wil beginnen met de internationale financi<91>le crisis en de rol van het toezicht daarin. De oorzaken van de financi<91>le crisis zijn velerlei en door een complexe samenloop van omstandigheden kwamen we dicht bij een ineenstorting van het internationale financi<91>le systeem. Krachtig ingrijpen door centrale banken en overheden wereldwijd heeft dit kunnen voorkomen, maar het had uiteraard nooit zo ver mogen komen. Als gevolg van de globalisering zijn steeds grotere, mondiaal opererende financi<91>le instellingen ontstaan, die ook onderling steeds meer met elkaar verweven zijn geraakt. Hierdoor is het systeemrisico in de financi<91>le sector sterk toegenomen en kon een hypotheekcrisis in de Verenigde Staten het mondiale financi<91>le systeem aan het wankelen brengen. Binnen het Koninkrijk is de financi<91>le sector in Nederland aanzienlijk zwaarder getroffen door de crisis dan die in de Nederlandse Antillen en Aruba. De Nederlandse staat heeft verschillende financi<91>le instellingen te hulp moeten schieten om ze van de ondergang te redden, wat zelfs tot nationalisatie van <8e><8e>n van de grootste banken heeft geleid. In de Nederlandse Antillen en Aruba hebben de financi<91>le instellingen uiteraard ook de gevolgen van de crisis gevoeld, zoals de waardedaling van beleggingsportefeuilles en de sterk gedaalde rentetarieven. Echter, door de geringere internationale ori<91>ntatie, de grotere risicoaversie en het toezichtbeleid van de BNA zijn onze lokale financi<91>le instellingen niet in problemen gekomen. De instellingen actief in de internationale financi<91>le en zakelijke dienstverlening zijn harder getroffen door de financi<91>le crisis als gevolg van hun sterke internationale ori<91>ntatie. Mede door het toezichtbeleid van de BNA zijn ook in deze sector geen instellingen in problemen gekomen, maar zijn de activiteiten wel afgenomen. Dit heeft bij verschillende instellingen geleid tot afslankingen, waaronder afvloeiing van personeel. Dames en heren, we moeten ons realiseren dat het toezicht op de financi<91>le sector altijd achter de feiten aanloopt. Ontwikkelingen in financi<91>le markten verlopen razend snel als gevolg van de globalisering en de voortschrijdende informatietechnologie. Nieuwe, vaak zeer complexe financi<91>le producten worden binnen korte tijd in de markt gezet met de belofte van aantrekkelijke rendementen zonder dat de risico<d5>s in voldoende mate worden doorgrond. Zolang de rendementen waargemaakt worden, blijft kritiek uit. Deze situatie verandert echter snel als het mis gaat en beleggers hun beleggingen aanzienlijk moeten afwaarderen, zoals met de derivaten gebaseerd op Amerikaanse hypotheken is gebeurd. Inadequaat risicobeheer, een scheefgegroeid beloningsbeleid en onvoldoende deskundigheid of alertheid van commissarissen van financi<91>le instellingen zijn enkele factoren die hebben bijgedragen aan de crisis. Deze factoren werden ook door de toezichthouders ge<95>dentificeerd en zijn onder de aandacht van de verantwoordelijke bewindslieden gebracht. Adequaat ingrijpen werd echter gehinderd door wettelijke beperkingen. Wetgevingsprocessen verlopen in het algemeen traag. Dit gaat zeker op voor toezichtwetgeving, die vaak erg technisch is en de gewone burger amper aanspreekt. Het is dus geen onderwerp waar politiek gescoord mee kan worden. Een crisis blijkt dan vaak een unieke kans om wetgeving snel aangenomen te krijgen. In het geval van de Nederlandse Antillen kan ik dat met een voorbeeld illustreren. Begin jaren negentig hadden wij gewerkt aan een wetsvoorstel om de bestaande toezichtwetgeving aanzienlijk te moderniseren ten einde adequater te kunnen optreden bij kredietinstellingen. Op een gegeven moment kwam een grote Venezolaanse bank in problemen die ook als offshore bank in de Nederlandse Antillen actief was. Deze crisis droeg er aan bij dat het wetsvoorstel binnen korte tijd werd behandeld en aangenomen. De toen ingevoerde landsverordening toezicht bank- en kredietwezen 1994 gaf de BNA het noodzakelijke wettelijke instrumentarium om effectiever bij onder toezicht staande instellingen in te grijpen. Hierdoor konden problemen bij instellingen sneller worden ge<95>dentificeerd en adequaat worden opgetreden om erger te voorkomen. Hopelijk zorgt de recente financi<91>le crisis ook voor een snelle behandeling en aanname van de binnenkort aangeboden harmonisatiewetgeving van het toezicht. Hiermee wordt het wettelijke toezichtinstrumentarium verder gemoderniseerd conform internationale normen en richtlijnen en worden overeenkomstige bepalingen in de verschillende toezichtwetten geharmoniseerd. Dit is van groot belang om onze positie als internationaal financieel dienstencentrum te kunnen handhaven en uitbouwen. Uit de financi<91>le crisis vallen een aantal lessen te trekken, die internationaal en binnen het Koninkrijk op korte termijn tot veranderingen in het toezicht op de financi<91>le sector kunnen leiden om de kans op herhaling aanzienlijk te verkleinen. Een selectie uit de belangrijkste voorstellen die circuleren. Ten eerste dient de rol van risicobeheersing bij financi<91>le instellingen substantieel te worden versterkt. In de periode v<97><97>r de crisis werd het risicomanagement steeds meer gemarginaliseerd ten gunste van de grote winsten belovende nieuwe complexe financi<91>le producten. Onder meer de BIS, het IMF en de Commissie Maas hebben inmiddels voorstellen gedaan om het risicomanagement te versterken door onder andere de oprichting van een risicocommissie bij financi<91>le instellingen en door de raad van commissarissen en de interne accountant een grotere rol te geven in het beoordelen van risico<d5>s. Ten tweede is het beloningsbeleid van de top van financi<91>le instellingen dringend aan revisie toe. Wereldwijd zijn de beloningspraktijken onder hevige kritiek komen te staan en initiatieven genomen om die te reguleren. Vooral de variabele component gekoppeld aan de winstgevendheid van de instelling heeft vanwege de verkeerde prikkels tot excessen geleid en dient te worden beperkt. De noodzakelijke aanpassingen zullen worden vertaald in algemene richtlijnen voor het beloningsbeleid in de financi<91>le sector. Ten derde is een meer evenwichtige belangenafweging binnen het beleid van financi<91>le instellingen noodzakelijk. V<97><97>r de crisis stond het belang van de aandeelhouders voorop en waren de belangen van andere stakeholders, zoals spaarders en werknemers, daaraan vaak ondergeschikt. Het bestuur van de instelling is in de eerste plaats verantwoordelijk voor een evenwichtige belangenafweging, waarbij waardecreatie op lange termijn voorop dient te staan. Ook op dit gebied zijn door internationale organisaties en commissies waardevolle aanbevelingen gedaan op basis waarvan concrete richtlijnen kunnen worden uitgevaardigd. Ten vierde is versterking van de kapitaalbuffers van financi<91>le instellingen noodzakelijk. Ondermeer collega Wellink in BIS verband, het IMF en de Financial Stability Board werken hard aan voorstellen. Gedacht wordt aan hogere kapitaaleisen in het algemeen, aangevuld met extra eisen voor grote internationale instellingen, die een zogenaamd systeemrisico inhouden. Verder wordt gepleit voor mechanismen die de kapitaalbuffers in goede tijden verplicht versterken om klappen in slechte tijden op te vangen. Financi<91>le instellingen moeten weerbaarder worden in tijden van crisis, zodat overheden niet meer massaal hoeven bij te springen om te voorkomen dat de financi<91>le stabiliteit van een land wordt ondermijnd. Als laatste punt wil ik de versterking van de corporate governance noemen. In dit kader speelt versterking van het toezicht door de raad van commissarissen een prominente rol. Om dit te realiseren dient de toezichthouder de deskundigheid en onafhankelijkheid van commissarissen in versterkte mate te toetsen, moeten audit en risk committees bij financi<91>le instellingen verplicht worden gesteld en dient het functioneren van de commissarissen op regelmatige basis te worden ge<91>valueerd. Dames en heren, voor behoud van gezonde internationale concurrentie-verhoudingen en een <d2>level playing field<d3> is het van essentieel belang dat toezichthouders wereldwijd nauw met elkaar samenwerken bij de uitwerking van de voorstellen in <d2>best practices<d3> die in nationale wet- en regelgeving voor het toezicht op financi<91>le instellingen moeten worden opgenomen. Internationale instellingen, zoals de BIS en het IMF, hebben hierin een voorstrekkers- en co<9a>rdinerende rol. Ook regionaal worden samenwerkingsinitiatieven ontplooid. In dit verband kan het initiatief om tot een Europees toezichtmodel te komen langs de lijnen uitgestippeld door het De Larosi<8f>re rapport worden genoemd. Wat mij in dit initiatief aanspreekt is dat de nationale toezichthouders verantwoordelijk blijven voor de uitvoering van het toezicht. Boven de nationale toezichthouders komt een Europees orgaan dat bindende beleidsregels opstelt, signalerend en bindend mag optreden bij conflicten tussen nationale toezichthouders in het geval van grensoverschrijdende financi<91>le instellingen en toeziet op een uniforme toepassing van wet- en regelgeving. Afdalend naar het Koninkrijksniveau pleit ik voor een soortgelijke toezichtstructuur, die ik nader voor u zal toelichten. Naast de uitdagingen die de financi<91>le crisis wereldwijd voor het toezicht op financi<91>le instellingen heeft gebracht, spelen dichter bij huis tevens de staatkundige veranderingen binnen het Koninkrijk. De huidige Nederlandse Antillen van vijf eilanden houdt op te bestaan. Cura<8d>ao en St. Maarten worden autonome landen binnen het Koninkrijk, terwijl Bonaire, Saba en St. Eustatius onderdeel worden van Nederland. Deze nieuwe structuur betekent dat het belang van grensoverschrijdende toezicht, ook al speelt het zich af op de kleine schaal binnen het Koninkrijk, toeneemt. Dit vergt een andere organisatie van het toezicht om de effectiviteit en de effici<91>ntie ervan te kunnen blijven waarborgen. In de huidige structuur van het Koninkrijk speelt grensoverschrijdend toezicht ook al een rol. Dit is bijvoorbeeld tussen de Nederlandse Antillen en Aruba het geval, omdat verschillende financi<91>le instellingen met het hoofdkantoor op Cura<8d>ao tevens vestigingen hebben op Aruba. Ook tussen de Nederlandse Antillen en Nederland is sprake van grensoverschrijdend toezicht; het gaat dan vooral om instellingen actief in de internationale financi<91>le dienstverlening. Om dit gemeenschappelijke toezicht beter te structureren heeft de Bank in het verleden al verschillende bilaterale samenwerkingsovereenkomsten met de Centrale Bank van Aruba en De Nederlandsche Bank afgesloten. Met de Centrale Bank van Aruba gaat het om de MOU<d5>s voor het toezicht op bank- en kredietinstellingen van 14 oktober 1998 en het toezicht op het verzekeringswezen van 3 april 2003. Voorafgaand aan deze MOU<d5>s werd al op 22 april 1998 een protocol voor periodieke consultaties tussen beide instellingen getekend. Met De Nederlandsche Bank werd op 28 augustus 1997 een MOU voor banktoezicht en op 3 april 2002 een MOU voor het toezicht op pensioenfondsen en verzekeringsmaatschappijen getekend. In maart 2008 is de samenwerking tussen de centrale banken van het Koninkrijk verder uitgebreid en ge<95>ntensiveerd met de ondertekening van een trilaterale MOU. Specifieke samenwerkingsgebieden betreffen integriteittoezicht, financi<91>le stabiliteit, toezicht op het betalingssysteem, invoering van het gewijzige Basel II kapitaalakkoord, statistieken, strategische planning en budgettering, training en uitwisseling van personeel. In de samenwerking ligt de nadruk op ondersteuning door De Nederlandsche Bank middels de uitwisseling van haar uitgebreide kennis en ervaring op deze gebieden met haar Caribische partners. Voorts is de organisatie van de samenwerking verder geformaliseerd en bestaat uit een Raad van Presidenten, ondersteund door een Technische Commissie die verantwoordelijk is voor de uitvoering van gemaakte afspraken en wordt bijgestaan door een secretaris. Met deze schets van de evolutie in de samenwerking tussen de centrale banken van het Koninkrijk wil ik illustreren dat de stap naar de organisatie van het toezicht op financi<91>le instellingen op Koninkrijksniveau eigenlijk helemaal niet een grote is en logisch volgt uit de steeds hechter wordende onderlinge samenwerking. De opzet die ik voor ogen heb voor dit Koninkrijks-toezichtorgaan, wat bijvoorbeeld het College van Koninkrijkstoezichthouders zou kunnen gaan heten, vertoont daarom analogie met de organisatie van de huidige trilaterale samenwerking. Het Koninkrijkstoezichtorgaan zal bestaan uit de presidenten van de centrale banken in het Koninkrijk, die uit hun midden een voorzitter kiezen. Dit orgaan zal worden bijgestaan door een Technische Commissie bestaande uit 3 leden. Elke centrale bank draagt <8e><8e>n lid voor, waarbij de directeur belast met toezicht wordt beoogd. De Technische Commissie, ondersteund door een secretariaat, draagt zorg voor de voorbereiding en bewaking van tijdige implementatie van wet- en regelgeving op het gebied van financieel toezicht in lijn met de internationale <d2>best practices<d3>, een <d2>level playing field<d3> met eerlijke concurrentie-verhoudingen, en naleving van de wet- en regelgeving binnen het Koninkrijk. De uitwerking van de benodigde wet- en regelgeving valt onder de verantwoordelijkheid van een uitvoerend orgaan, waarin de onderdirecteuren van de verschillende toezichtdisciplines zitting hebben. Dit orgaan is tevens verantwoordelijk voor de daadwerkelijke uitvoering van het overeengekomen beleid en controleert of de wet- en regelgeving in de landen van het Koninkrijk wordt nageleefd. De door mij geschetste organisatiestructuur van het toezicht op financi<91>le instellingen in het Koninkrijk zal de naleving van internationale standaarden en de toepassing van uniforme regels binnen het Koninkrijk kunnen garanderen. Zo zal bijvoorbeeld de huidige problematiek rond de negatieve FATF-evaluatie van het toezicht op Aruba in de nieuwe toezichtstructuur niet meer mogen voorkomen. Voorts zal de voorgestelde structuur de transparantie en geloofwaardigheid van het toezicht bevorderen. Bovendien siert het het Koninkrijk als alle partners voldoen aan de internationale eisen met betrekking tot het financi<91>le toezicht. In het kader van de staatkundige veranderingen in het Caribische deel van het Koninkrijk vindt momenteel al intensieve samenwerking plaats tussen de toezichthouders in de Nederlandse Antillen en Nederland om de overgang naar de nieuwe situatie zo soepel mogelijk te laten verlopen. Hoewel de staatkundige grenzen binnen het Koninkrijk zullen veranderen, blijven de financi<91>le sectoren op de eilanden in het Caribische deel nauw met elkaar verweven. Uniforme wet- en regelgeving en beleid op het gebied van toezicht op de financi<91>le instellingen die actief zijn op de eilanden kan er dan voor zorgen dat de toezichtlasten voor de instellingen beheersbaar blijven en een <d2>level playing field<d3> kan worden gehandhaafd. Institutionalisering van de organisatie van het toezicht in een Koninkrijksorgaan kan de duurzaamheid hiervan bevorderen. Een voorbeeld in dit kader is het gedragstoezicht, dat in Nederland al geruime tijd gemeengoed is maar in de Cariben nog in de kinderschoenen staat. Aangezien de BES-eilanden onder de verantwoordelijk-heid van Nederland komen te vallen, zullen de financi<91>le instellingen op deze eilanden ook met gedragstoezicht te maken krijgen. Dankzij de hechte samenwerking binnen het Koninkrijksorgaan kunnen Cura<8d>ao, St. Maarten en Aruba dan gelijk optrekken met de BES-eilanden, zodat een <d2>level playing field<d3> kan worden gehandhaafd. Dames en heren, het is niet zo moeilijk een schets te presenteren over hoe het toezicht op de financi<91>le sector in het Koninkrijk het best georganiseerd kan worden. De werkelijke uitdaging zit in de concrete uitwerking ervan, waarbij de nodige barri<8f>res overwonnen moeten worden. Zo dient de wet- en regelgeving op het gebied van toezicht zoveel mogelijk uniform te zijn, maar tevens rekening te houden met de verscheidenheid van de Koninkrijkspartners. Met andere woorden: "eenheid in verscheidenheid." Dit uitgangspunt moet ervoor zorgen dat het toezicht in alle delen van het Koninkrijk voldoet aan de internationale normen, maar ruimte laat voor onderlinge verschillen op grond van bijvoorbeeld de structuur en ontwikkelingsgraad van de financi<91>le sector. Daarnaast krijgen we in de nieuwe staatkundige structuur te maken met vier landen, vier parlementen en vier toezichtorganen. Het zal dan geen eenvoudige opgave zijn om vrijwel uniforme wetgeving op hetzelfde tijdstip in alle delen van het Koninkrijk in te voeren, wat het beoogde <d2>level playing field<d3> in gevaar kan brengen. Ik zie hier voor het Koninkrijkstoezichtorgaan een belangrijke voorbereidende en co<9a>rdinerende rol weggelegd. Dames en heren, ik kijk uit naar een vruchtbare discussie met u over de toekomst van het toezicht in de Nederlandse Cariben in het bijzonder en het Koninkrijk in het algemeen. Een toekomst die wij grotendeels in eigen hand hebben. Door nog intensiever met elkaar samen te werken, kunnen wij de uitdagingen van de financi<91>le crisis en de staatkundige veranderingen voor het toezicht op de financi<91>le instellingen in het Koninkrijk met vertrouwen tegemoet treden. Aan ons is de taak om deze uitdagingen uit te werken in een solide toezichtraamwerk dat bijdraagt aan gezonde financi<91>le instellingen en financi<91>le stabiliteit in de landen van het Koninkrijk. Ik dank u voor uw aandacht en wens u een succesvol seminar toe.

Title: Pensions
CentralBank: Central Bank of Curaao and Sint Maarten
text: The implications of the financial and economic crisis for the financial services industry Download the powerpoint-presentation Speech by Mr. Alberto Romero on the occasion of the 2010 Globalaw Americas Regional Meeting, June 11, 2010 Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. It is a pleasure for me to join you today on the occasion of the 2010 Globalaw Americas Regional Meeting. Today I would like to share with you my views on the implications of the financial and economic crisis for the financial services industry. Ladies and gentlemen, the first decade of this new millennium has seemingly been jam-packed with crises and turmoil around the world. The decade started off with the dotcom crisis, which resulted in a spectacular drop in the value of international stock exchanges in the major financial centers. In 2006, prices in the housing markets in the United States reached their peak after which real estate values plummeted by at least 20%. During 2007, many hedge funds operating in important financial centers were faced with liquidity and capitalization problems, resulting in the liquidation of several funds and a staggering loss of value for their shareholders. The next crisis that knocked on our doors was the international financial crisis in 2008-2009. This crisis has had the most implications for the United States, Europe, and the Asian markets. As we speak today, many Southern European countries are facing major troubles because of mounting public debt and difficulties accessing capital markets to finance their growing budget deficits. In addition, the debt problem of Greece is threatening the role of the Euro as the second reserve currency in the world. The financial crisis and the economic disequilibria affecting us today are not new phenomena. During the 1980s, the Latin American countries of Argentina and Brazil were faced with similar problems. The current financial problems of Greece, Portugal, Spain, Italy, Ireland (the so-called PIIGS) - all forming part of the Euro area - are a good example of how disequilibria in one country can spread to other countries. More specifically, the situation in Greece today is a good case study because it reveals how consistently weak management of public finances over a period of years leads to rising public debt. Fiscal budgets were approved year after year in Greece despite the fact that they were not in accordance with the budgetary agreements of the stability pact for the countries using the Euro. Today Greece has a public debt-to-GDP ratio of 120% and a budget deficit of 14% of GDP. Consequently, the country is forced to pay 13.5% interest on 2-year government bonds in the international financial markets. Greeced5s experiences provide a clear example of how badly managed economies will in the end produce serious problems for the authorities of these countries. Responsible, sound, and safe management of public funds is the only viable way to stay out of difficulty in the long run and to avoid having to pay a high price for the refinancing of outstanding debt instruments. Ladies and gentlemen, in my presentation today I will highlight three topics. I will start by giving you an overview of the importance of the financial services industry of Cura8dao for the islandd5s economy and the specific challenges facing the local authorities in the immediate future. Given the changing environment and how the international financial community perceives the financial services rendered by small jurisdictions like ours, we have to be responsive to these perceptions and work to comply fully with current international tax standards. The common trend today in this area seems to be the continuously growing exchange of information among countries. Global actions aimed at achieving closer cooperation between countries to avoid harmful taxation will without a doubt determine the agenda in the coming years. The second topic that I would like to elaborate on is the situation in the global economy and developments in the financial markets. What are the risks and threats of the financial crisis, and what have we learned from it? One thing is clear: despite the negative impact of the financial crisis around the world, our economy has weathered this crisis well. According to preliminary data, our economy expanded by 1% (GDP growth) in 2009, while the unemployment rate dropped below 10% for the first time in decades. Last, I will discuss some implications of the credit crisis for the financial and particularly the banking industry. What are the most important lessons to be learned, and how committed are we to work together to avoid future crisis situations? Ladies and gentlemen, the financial services industry is one of Cura8daod5s major economic sectors in terms of value added, employment, and foreign exchange generation. On average, the financial intermediation sector contributes 16% to GDP. A sectoral breakdown reveals that domestic banks contribute 5.4% to GDP, insurance and pension funds, 5.2%, international financial services, 2.5%, and other financial services, 3.1%. Moreover, during the 2005d02008 period, financial intermediation contributed roughly 7% to total employment. The international financial services in particular are important in terms of foreign exchange generation as they contribute on average 11% to the total foreign exchange revenues from the exports of goods and services. It should be noted, however, that these exportshave been declining gradually from 12% in 2000 to 7% in 2008. Considering the importance of the financial industry for our economy, global trends in the financial industry will be a major challenge Cura8daod5s authorities will have to face. In addition, our authorities must be able to cope with the many local developments to insure that Cura8daod5s competitiveness is supported and boosted as much as possible in the future. The ongoing constitutional reform is one of the major local developments affecting Cura8daod5s economy. It is important to note that the new country of Cura8dao will enjoy the same internal autonomy the Netherlands Antilles currently enjoys. The challenge will be for the new country of Cura8dao to continue using the existing infrastructure that consists of, among other things, the current financial and legal framework and international treaties of the Netherlands Antilles, to promote and support the islandd5s economic development. Once the central government is dismantled, the two- tier government system that we have known for so many years will become a part of the past. In its place, the government of the country of Cura8dao will consist of a mix of civil servants from both the central government and the island government of Cura8dao. In addition, the new entity will have to make sure it continues to comply with the new budgetary and financial norms agreed upon with the Netherlands and the implementation and enforcement of the new corporate government rules. Maintaining a financial industry that is healthy, flexible, and transparent is another major challenge Cura8dao and other financial centers are facing and will continue to face in the future. Since 2008, international tax transparency and information exchange standards have been very high on the political agenda. This development is a result of the many financial scandals that have negatively affected several countries worldwide. In addition, the global financial crisis highlighted the relevance of maintaining healthy and transparent financial centers. The G20 has made tax transparency one of the major discussion items at its last several meetings, stating that action will be taken against non-cooperative jurisdictions, including tax havens. The general consensus is that the era of banking secrecy is over and that sanctions will be taken against those who do not meet international standards for the exchange of tax information. The OECD (Organization of Economic Cooperation and Development) periodically publishes a list of countries that the Global Forum has assessed as against the implementation of the international tax standard in their jurisdiction. Information exchange requires that jurisdictions enter into international agreements to be in a position to provide administrative assistance in all tax matters. Since 2009, many agreements have been signed by jurisdictions previously labeled by the OECD as not substantially implementing the information exchange standard. We can be very proud that the Netherlands Antilles was removed from the grey list of the OECD in September 2009. Consequently, the Netherlands Antilles is now listed among the 72 jurisdictions--including many developed countries--that have substantially implemented the internationally agreed upon tax standard. Furthermore, the Netherlands Antilles is currently negotiating with several countries to reach agreements aimed at avoiding double taxation and at the exchange of tax information. In line with developments in the international financial industry, the CIFA ( Curacao International Financial Services Association) has focused on developing a unified vision and strategy for the financial services industry to make sure Cura8dao can maximize the opportunities available to the island. CIFAd5s vision is to make Cura8dao the gateway of choice, both inbound and outbound, for channeling cross-border international financial services transactions with Latin American countries, such as Argentina, Brazil, Mexico, and Venezuela. For Cura8dao to become a premier and globally competitive financial services center and to reach the status of one of the top ten financial services centers in the world, the current tax treaties network of the Netherlands Antilles should be expanded. However, the core business of Cura8daod5s international financial sector currently consists mainly of services based on tax benefits, characterized by a very limited amount of company activity. Therefore, the authorities of Cura8dao should aim to create onshore structures with d4substanced5. Compliance and substance are the two key factors Cura8dao should focus on. This focus does not necessarily imply the total elimination of low corporate tax rates. It does imply the promotion of transparency and elimination of the perception of being a low tax jurisdiction, in order to shift away from being a d2tax havend3 to becoming an d2investor havend3. This shift could be accomplished through the introduction and promotion of new niche products and services and the expansion of the Dutch Caribbean Securities Exchange (DCSE). The launch of the DCSE in the beginning of 2010 was an important step towards achieving our goal of providing an exchange that offers time- and cost-efficient listings for international corporations and investment funds and an alternative to the Anglo-Saxon exchanges in other jurisdictions. To achieve our ultimate objective, however, additional conditions must be met. These conditions include reducing the corporate tax rate, cultivating a strong and professional labor force, making our labor market more flexible to improve our competitiveness, investing in state-of-the-art technology, and moving towards providing red carpet services. By creating the necessary framework that complies with international standards and provides business services with d4substanced5, we will be able to offer investors a safe, secure, and flexible business environment, one that may become an important hub for the regional head offices of international enterprises. Ladies and gentlemen, as I indicated, my second topic today is current developments in the global economy and the financial markets. In an effort to prevent a collapse of the global financial system, authorities, particularly in advanced economies, took extraordinary measures aimed at supporting demand and reducing uncertainty and systemic risk in financial markets. These measures included the expansion of retail deposit insurance schemes and the provision of guarantees for bank liabilities other than deposits. In addition, banks received billions in capital injections and guarantees for their assets in return for government ownership stakes. Central banks also provided generous liquidity support and cut interest rates. Nevertheless, these efforts could not prevent a worldwide recession. Overall, the global economy contracted by 0.6% in 2009. Output contracted in most of the advanced economies, including the United States and the Euro area. In addition, economic activities slowed in the emerging markets and developing economies. As a consequence, many economies experienced a significant increase in unemployment. Fortunately, global economic growth has rebounded recently, and financial conditions have improved. According to the International Monetary Fundd5s most recent World Economic Outlook, global growth is projected to expand by about 4. % in 2010 and 2011. However, the pace of recovery differs across and within regions. Economic growth in emerging and developing countries is projected to be strong, reaching around 6. % in 2010 as inventory investment expands, led by prospects of improved demand in both advanced and emerging economies. In addition, growth in countries such as Brazil, China, and India is picking up as a result of increased capital inflows. In contrast, the advanced economies, are projected to recover only moderately by around 2. % in 2010 and 2011 following a decline of about 3% in 2009. This sluggish performance will be due largely to weak private demand. Private consumption in the United States, which was the main driver of growth before the crisis, is recovering slowly as consumers are being more prudent. Meanwhile, private demand growth in Europe is hampered by the weak banking sector that limits credit supply. When we take a closer look at Europe, i.e., the euro area, it seems that we have begun a new episode in the international financial crisis. The first phase of the crisis started with the subprime mortgage-related turmoil in 2007 and affected mainly the financial markets. During the second phase, the financial crisis spread into the real sector causing trade, consumption, and investment to fall worldwide. Now, we have reached the third stage in which the financial markets have started to question the sustainability of economic policies, particularly in light of the dire state of public finances. As a consequence, the financial markets have started to question the sustainability of the economic recovery itself. This third phase has hit Europe in particular and has resulted in a strong decline of the euro. The current problems in Europe, and in the euro area in particular, are related to three factors: (1) a credit boom in certain countries including Greece, Spain, and Portugal due to lower interest rates after these countries joined the eurozone; (2) a lack of risk management in economic policy in these countries; and (3) the fact that the Stability and Growth Pact was neither adhered to nor enforced, despite its being the cornerstone of the European monetary union. Public deficits in these countries have been increasing over the past several years due to shortsighted fiscal and economic policy. National economic policy rarely included long-term strategies to improve the countriesd5 competitiveness. In addition, public finances deteriorated even more during 2008 and 2009 as a result of public sector interventions to avoid a collapse of the financial sectors. Greece has been registering high borrowings and debt for many years, mainly because the country overspent while its revenues fell. As a consequence, Greece became highly indebted and has lost about 25% of its competitiveness since the adoption of the euro. By the end of 2009, the general public deficit in Greece had reached 13.6% of GDP, and public debt had increased to 115% of GDP, the highest debt burden in the euro area. Given these numbers, the financial markets stopped lending to Greece, forcing it to appeal to the European Union and the International Monetary Fund for assistance. Greece has now adopted a major adjustment program, which includes structural reforms and fiscal adjustments. Given the debt crisis in Greece, investors currently prefer dollar-denominated assets to euro- denominated assets. Confidence in the euro remains shaky despite the measures taken to ease the situation in Greece because Portugal, Italy, Ireland, and Spain also are faced with high deficits and mounting public debt, fueling fears of contagion. Amidst worries that the European monetary union is on its last leg, and news that some countries, for example Iran and China, are planning to sell their euro reserves, the euro has been declining sharply against the US dollar, dropping 15% so far this year. As is often the case in times of financial turmoil, many investors have been buying gold because the metal is considered a d2safe havend3. Due to investors seeking to protect their wealth amid Europed5s sovereign-debt crisis, gold reached a record price of 1,249.40 an ounce on May 14th, 2010. According to predictions, it may trade at 1,400 to 1,600 an ounce in the next two years. The current unhealthy financial situation of many governments has led to appeals for not only broader supervision of banks, but also for (1) a restructuring of the banking sector, which would prevent banks from investing in certain derivatives and trading with their own money, and (2) measures to make sure banks pay for any future financial meltdowns they cause. The general concern is that in the past, banks relied too much on the implicit guarantee that they would be d2savedd3 through government intervention, and that, therefore, they took too many risks. Consequently, both in Europe and in the United States, legislation is now being drafted to make banks increase their share of equity drastically, and to force them to contribute to emergency funds that can be used to limit future banking crises. Banks can be made to contribute to such funds either through special bank taxes levied on a share of their outstanding liabilities, or by taxing certain financial transactions. No matter which approach is taken, the aim is clear: to end the situation in which financial institutions pocket the profits they make when they take excessive risks, and if they incur big losses, the taxpayer is forced to pay the bill. (d2Privatize profits and socialize lossesd3) Ladies and gentlemen, the third and final topic I would like to highlight today is the implications of the credit crisis for the financial and the banking industry. The recent financial crisis has taught us some critical lessons and has revealed some important weaknesses of the global financial system. As we all know, innovation in the financial sector resulted in the development of new instruments that were supposed to expand the diversification of the risk for savers and investors. However, financial regulation was not equipped to detect the risk concentration and flawed incentives behind these innovations. In fact, regulators were not aware of the underlying risks of the financial innovations and the interconnectedness between activities and institutions. As a consequence, financial institutions and other investors took risky decisions beyond the regulatory net. The financial crisis has made us more aware of the negative externalities that financial innovation and financial globalization can create. One important lesson that can be drawn from this crisis is that markets cannot function properly without effective regulation and supervision. Therefore, there is now a general consensus that financial sector regulation has to be strengthened and broadened in order to prevent similar financial sector crises in the future. Generally, five areas are recognized where actions should be taken. First, financial regulation should be broadened to include all financial activities that pose economy-wide risks. Second, capital regulation and liquidity and risk management have to reflect both individual institution risks and their potential to form systemic risk. Hence, regulation should also have to focus on strengthening financial institutionsd5 management of liquidity and risk. Third, a macro-prudential approach to regulation is required. Traditionally, financial sector regulation has been centered on the stability of individual institutions. However, a macro-prudential approach that considers the systemic implications of the collective behavior of financial institutions also is needed. Fourth, information disclosure and corporate governance practices need to improve to enhance market discipline. As for information disclosure, derivative market instruments in particular need to be subject to greater transparency. In the area of corporate governance practices, conflicts of interest must be reduced by making remuneration schemes or bonuses more consistent with long-term success instead of short-term profits. And fifth, there is a need for greater coordination across countries in both the design of regulation and the monitoring of systemic risk. The recent financial crisis has emphasized the need for international cooperation and policy coordination. As financial markets have become increasingly integrated and financial centers interconnected, no country can escape the effects of a financial crisis, no matter where it occurs. Hence, financial sector regulation and supervision cannot stop at the national borders. In fact, recent experience in dealing with the crisis has shown us that international policy coordination can be very effective. Cooperation and policy coordination in the areas of financial sector supervision and regulation also are crucial on the Kingdom level. To address our financial sectord5s vulnerabilities, a financial supervisory structure in which every country within the Kingdom will have its own supervisory institution, complemented by a standard-setting body at the Kingdom level or Committee of Kingdom Supervisors, is recommended. This body should consist of the presidents of the respective central banks and should be in charge of preparing legislation in line with international best practices, the timely implementation of rules and regulations, and monitoring compliance. Such a structure will guarantee compliance with international supervisory standards. In addition, this structure will create a level playing field with uniform rules within the Kingdom and promote credibility and transparency. The existing cooperative agreements between the central banks of the Netherlands, Aruba, and the Netherlands Antilles can serve as a basis for the development of a firm supervisory architecture and the achievement of sound financial institutions and financial stability in the new countries of the Kingdom. Ladies and gentlemen, today I had the pleasure of sharing my views with you on the implications of the financial and economic sector for the financial services industry. First, I discussed the importance of the financial services industry of Cura8dao and the challenges local authorities will have to face in the future. Next, I highlighted the situation in the global economy and developments in the financial markets. Finally, I reviewed the implications of the credit crisis for the financial and the banking industry. The conclusions that we can draw today from all this are as follows - 1.The regulation and supervision of the financial services sector will need to be strengthened and broadened to prevent similar crises in the future. - 2.Banks and other financial institutions will become subject to stricter supervision to prevent them from taking excessive risks, possibly through mandatory higher equity levels. In addition, they will be forced to contribute to emergency funds that can be used in case of financial turmoil. - 3.Top management bonuses will become more long-term oriented; quick profits and quick bonuses will become a thing of the past. - 4.Both at the local and international levels, cooperation and policy coordination in the areas of financial sector supervision and regulation are crucial to achieve and maintain financial system stability. - 5.The role of the Euro in the world depends heavily on how well the euro area is able to manage its deficits and outstanding debt. Without proper budget discipline, the euro will lose its value, and hence, its role as the worldd5s second reserve currency. Thank you for your attention!

text: Bancaribe 30 years of relations Curazolenas - Venezuelans in a dynamic and challenging environment Speech by Dr. Emsley D. Tromp on the occasion of the presentation of the book "Curacao and Venezuela united by the Caribbean" Auditorium, Bank van de Nederlandse Antillen; June 22, 2010 Good evening ladies and gentlemen, First of all, I would like to congratulate the management and management staff of "Bancaribe Curacao Bank N.V." on the occasion of the thirtieth anniversary of this financial institution. In order to commemorate this important milestone, Bancaribe has published the book "Curacao and Venezuela united by the Caribbean". This book provides us with more depth into the strong historical, geopolitical and economic ties between Curacao and Venezuela dating back many centuries. I would like to congratulate the authors of the various articles for the documentation and in-depth analysis of the relationship between Curacao and Venezuela. The thirty-year presence of Bancaribe on our island is certainly one of the evidences of the strong ties, particularly of the economic ties between Curacao and Venezuela. Ladies and gentlemen, the strong economic ties are reflected by the trade relations between Venezuela and the Netherlands Antilles in general and with Curacao in particular. In fact, with 14% of the total exports and imports of the Netherlands Antilles, Venezuela is one of our largest trading partners after the United States and the Netherlands. During the period 2000 to 2009, Venezuela contributed an average of 16 per cent per year to total foreign exchange earnings from exports of goods and services in the Netherlands Antilles. The main contributors to Venezuela's foreign exchange earnings are the exporting companies of the free zone for Venezuela, the lease fees paid by PDVSA to cover the operating expenses of the refinery in Curacao and the consumption of Venezuelan tourists. Meanwhile, Venezuela's merchandise imports account for an average of 14% of total imports in the Netherlands Antilles. Venezuelan companies also play an important role in Curacao's international financial services industry, as one-third of the international banks operating in that sector are Venezuelan. Over three decades, companies operating in that sector, including Bancaribe, have faced different setbacks. A major setback was the termination of the Tax Treaty with the United States and the "U.S. Abolition of Foreign Tax Withholding" in 1985. In addition, the sector was adversely affected by developments, such as the gradual termination of tax arrangements in the Netherlands Antilles and increasing competition from tax-exempt tax jurisdictions. These developments resulted in a steady decline in the activities of the international financial services industries. Despite this decline, the sector remains of relative importance in the economy of the Netherlands Antilles. For example, during the period 2000-2009, this sector contributed on average approximately 10% to foreign exchange earnings from the export of goods and services. In addition, the international financial services sector has a high value-added component and broadens our economic base, making us less dependent on the tourism sector. Ladies and gentlemen, new opportunities have arisen for institutions in the international financial sector such as globalization and innovation in financial markets, and have resulted in the development of new market niches and products. However, the recent international financial crisis has shown us the negative externalities to which financial innovations and globalization can lead us. One of the main lessons to be drawn from the crisis is that financial markets cannot function well without proper regulation and supervision. Moreover, because of globalisation, regulation and supervision can no longer be limited to national borders. Recent experience in dealing with the crisis has shown us that international policy coordination and cooperation can indeed be very effective. There are generally five areas that require action: First, regulation should be expanded to include all activities that pose risks to the entire economy. Second, financial regulation will need to focus on strengthening the management of liquidity and risk financial institutions. Third, conflicts of interest must be reduced by making rewards that are more consistent with long-term success rather than short-term benefits. Fourth, the transparency of the financial system must be improved. And fifth, in the area of financial supervision, the goal should be to detect developments in the financial sector that could lead to a systemic crisis. Not only banks, but all financial institutions should be subject to strict and comprehensive supervision on a consolidated, firm and comprehensive basis. Certainly, this general trend towards broader financial supervision and regulation, and greater international policy cooperation and coordination, will have implications for our financial sector supervision. By ignoring international supervisory and regulatory standards, we risk being blacklisted, undermining confidence in our financial sector and investment climate. In small, open economies like ours, international policy cooperation and coordination in the areas of financial sector supervision and regulation are critical to international recognition and make us less vulnerable to future shocks . In our particular case, cooperation and policy coordination are also crucial at the Kingdom level. As I have already indicated on several occasions, I envisage a financial supervision structure in which each country within the Kingdom will have its own supervisory institution, complemented by a regulatory body at the Dutch united level or the Kingdom Committee of Supervisors. This normative body should be in charge of preparing legislation in line with international best practices, timely application of rules and regulations, and monitoring compliance. This structure ensures compliance with international supervisory standards. In addition, this structure will create a level playing field with uniform rules in the Kingdom and promote credibility and transparency. Looking to the near future, I see new opportunities for institutions in the international financial services sector. In September 2009, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) removed the Netherlands Antilles from the grey list of non-cooperative tax havens as a result of our efforts to implement OECD standards on transparency and exchange of information. As the development of the international financial services industry depends largely on how the sector is perceived by the rest of the world, the removal of the Netherlands Antilles from the OECD grey list makes our sector more credible and creates more opportunities for the future development of the industry. In addition, the Netherlands Antilles is currently negotiating with several countries to reach agreements aimed at avoiding double taxation and on the exchange of tax information. Ladies and gentlemen, we are in the final stage of dismantling the Netherlands Antilles. In a few months, Curacao and Sint Maarten will become autonomous countries within the Dutch Kingdom, while Bonaire, Saba and Saint Eustatius will become special municipalities of the Netherlands. As an autonomous country, Curacao will be able to address economic and social issues in a more specific context about the island, which could also be beneficial for the international financial services sector. With regard to this particular industry, some key policy areas need to be targeted to improve the competitiveness of the sector and make it more attractive to investors. For example, in the area of taxation, corporate tax must be reduced. What's more, our strength We need to improve the quality of our workforce. In addition, we must remove the current administrative barriers and bureaucracy that weaken our competitiveness as a place of investment. Over the past 30 years, the international financial services industry has faced obstacles, challenges, opportunities and rapid change. Bancaribe has proven to be a strong and reliable player in this dynamic and sometimes turbulent. I would like to express my gratitude for Bancaribe's confidence in the Netherlands Antilles and Curacao and as demonstrated by its continued presence for 30 years. I am looking forward to its continued presence in the international financial services industry and expanding our fruitful supervisory cooperation with the common goal of developing Curacao as a major international financial center. Thank you for your attention.

Tromp con ocasi<97>n de la presentaci<97>n del libro <d2>Curazao y Venezuela unidos por el Caribe<d3> Auditorium, Bank van de Nederlandse Antillen; Junio 22, 2010 Buenas noches se<96>oras y se<96>ores, Ante todo, yo quisiera felicitar la gerencia y el personal directivo del <d2>Bancaribe Curazao Bank N.V.<d3> con ocasi<97>n del trig<8e>simo aniversario de esta instituci<97>n financiera. Este libro nos proporciona m<87>s profundidad en los fuertes lazos hist<97>ricos, geopol<92>ticos y econ<97>micos entre Curazao y Venezuela que data de muchos siglos. Yo quisiera felicitar los autores de los distintos art<92>culos por la documentaci<97>n y an<87>lisis de fondo de la relaci<97>n entre Curazao y Venezuela. La presencia de treinta a<96>os de Bancaribe en nuestra isla es desde luego una de las evidencias de los fuertes lazos, particularmente de los lazos econ<97>micos entre Curazao y Venezuela. Damas y Caballeros, los fuertes lazos econ<97>micos son reflejados por las relaciones comerciales entre Venezuela y las Antillas Neerlandesas en general y con Curazao en particular. De hecho, con el 14% del total de las exportaciones e importaciones de las Antillas Neerlandesas, Venezuela es uno de nuestros mayores socios comerciales despu<8e>s de los Estados Unidos y Los Pa<92>ses Bajos. Durante del per<92>odo 2000 al 2009 Venezuela contribuy<97> con un promedio de 16% al a<96>o, al total de ingresos de divisas de las exportaciones de bienes y servicios en las Antillas Neerlandesas. Los principales contribuyentes a los ingresos de divisas de Venezuela son las compa<96><92>as exportadores de la zona franca para Venezuela, las cuotas de arrendamiento pagadas por PDVSA para cubrir los gastos operacionales de la refiner<92>a en Curazao y el consumo de los turistas Venezolanos. Entretanto, las importaciones de mercanc<92>as de Venezuela cuentan con un promedio de 14% del total de importaciones en las Antillas Neerlandesas. Compa<96><92>as Venezolanas tambi<8e>n desempe<96>an un papel importante en la industria de servicios financieros internacionales de Curazao, comoquiera que un tercio de los bancos internacionales que operaen ese sector son de Venezuela. A trav<8e>s de tres d<8e>cadas, compa<96><92>as operando en ese sector, incluyendo Bancaribe, han enfrentado diferentes contratiempos. Un contratiempo mayor fue la terminaci<97>n del Tratado Fiscal con los Estados Unidos y la <d2>Abolici<97>n Estadounidense de Retenci<97>n de Impuestos Extranjeros<d3> en 1985. Adem<87>s el sector se vio afectado negativamente por desarrollos, tal como la terminaci<97>n gradual de los acuerdos fiscales de la Antillas Neerlandesas y la competencia creciente de jurisdicciones fiscales exentas de impuestos. Estos desarrollos dieron lugar a una disminuci<97>n constante en las actividades de las industrias de servicios financieros internacionales. No obstante esta disminuci<97>n, el sector sigue teniendo una importancia relativa en la econom<92>a de las Antillas Neerlandesas. Por ejemplo, durante el per<92>odo 2000-2009, ese sector contribuy<97> como promedio con aproximadamente el 10 por ciento a los ingresos de divisas por la exportaci<97>n de bienes y servicios. Adem<87>s, el sector de servicios financieros internacionales tiene un alto componente de valor a<96>adido y ampl<92>a nuestra base econ<97>mica, lo que hace que dependamos menos del sector tur<92>stico. Se<96>oras y se<96>ores, han surgido nuevas oportunidades para las instituciones en el sector financiero internacional como la globalizaci<97>n y la innovaci<97>n de los mercados financieros, y se han traducido en el desarrollo de nuevos nichos de mercado y productos. Sin embargo, la reciente crisis financiera internacional nos ha demostrado las externalidades negativas a donde las innovaciones financieras y la globalizaci<97>n nos pueden conducir. Una de las principales lecciones que se puede extraer de la crisis, es que mercados financieros no pueden funcionar bien sin regulaci<97>n y supervisi<97>n apropiada. Adem<87>s, por motivo de la globalizaci<97>n, la regulaci<97>n y la supervisi<97>n ya no se puede ser limitada m<87>s a fronteras nacionales. La reciente experiencia del tratamiento de la crisis nos ha demostrado que la coordinaci<97>n y cooperaci<97>n de pol<92>tica internacional de hecho pueden ser muy efectivas.
